In their 2014 book The Second Machine Age, academics Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee identify the productivity explosion of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as the First Machine Age. Whereas technological innovations before the Industrial MRevolution were primarily augmentations of an individual’s capacity, the Industrial Revolution created tools that far exceeded their maker. From the synergy of the productive ensemble came such material abundance that a person living after was to a person living before almost as if an entirely new species.

Now try to imagine what would happen if the thing that built that system, the human brain, was in the process of undergoing a transformation analogous to it. The result would not be another technological revolution on the scale of the previous one. Once machines become inventors of better machines, the whole system will begin to compound recursively. The growth curve will go supernova, and beyond that point, any attempt to understand the scale of the transformation we’re talking about would be less science fiction than literal metaphysics.

This incomprehensibly vast transformation would be the climax of what Brynjolfsson and McAfee call the Second Machine Age. Just as the Industrial Revolution transcended the limits of human physical capacity, the ongoing information revolution is in the process of transcending human cognitive capacity.

To appreciate what that will mean, it’s helpful to revisit the intellectual roots of the Second Machine Age. They go back further than you might think. The first programmable machine was invented early in the nineteenth century by a mathematician named Charles Babbage. While his “Difference Engine” did nothing more than mechanically compute mathematical tables, his designed-but-never-built “Analytical Engine” was a general-purpose mechanical computer. Babbage laid the groundwork, but the true significance of his design remained hidden until his friend and collaborator, Ada Lovelace, saw how it could be extended to perform manipulations on arbitrary symbols. “The Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns,” she wrote in 1843, “just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.”

A century later, Alan Turing supplied this idea with a secure mathematical foundation by proving that any sufficiently general machine could simulate any other machine, effectively giving birth to the idea of software. After WWII, advancements in computer science came rapidly. Claude Shannon’s 1948 article on the “Mathematical Theory of Communication” separated information from meaning, thus allowing it to be measured, encoded, stored, and transmitted. Meanwhile, Vannevar Bush imagined a clever means of simplifying knowledge retrieval. In 1945, he described a hypothetical “memex” machine, a consolidated personal microfilm library with “trails” between documents. The idea impressed computer scientist Ted Nelson, who extended it to the notion of a “hypertext” in the 1960s, thereby creating the possibility of a web of interlinked documents like the one Tim Berners-Lee eventually invented in 1989.

Meanwhile, attendees at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop established AI as an independent research field. Their proposal famously conjectured that “every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” Early researchers pursued symbolic reasoning systems with real but limited successes.

These early symbolic systems that were reliant on rigid rules and hand-coded logic soon hit a wall when confronted with the messy, informal reality of the real world. As initial optimism curdled into missed deadlines and unfulfilled promises, funding evaporated, plunging the field into its first "AI winter." A brief revival in the 1980s via commercial expert systems triggered a second winter when those brittle architectures proved too expensive and difficult to maintain at scale.

The path back into the light began in the 1990s and early 2000s, driven not by pre-baked rules, but by data and statistical learning. The sudden explosion of the World Wide Web provided unprecedented volumes of digital text and information. Search engine pioneers like Google built algorithms like PageRank and probabilistic models to index, retrieve, and structure human knowledge at massive scale. Rather than teaching a machine how to think from scratch, search engines demonstrated the power of statistical pattern matching across vast repositories of existing human thought.

This statistical foundation set the stage for the deep learning revolution of the 2010s. Powered by modern graphics processing units (GPUs) and massive datasets like ImageNet, multi-layered artificial neural networks began performing perception tasks such as image recognition and speech processing with near-human precision. By shifting the paradigm from hand-engineered features to representation learning, deep learning proved that machines could automatically discover complex patterns in raw data, moving AI out of academic labs and into everyday consumer technologies.

Most recently, the field has undergone another profound shift with the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs). Building on transformer architectures, LLMs scale deep learning to billions of parameters trained on nearly the entire written corpus of humanity. In doing so, they have bridged the gap between pure statistical pattern matching and fluid natural language reasoning. By synthesizing knowledge, generating human-grade language, and adapting to novel tasks with minimal instruction, these models represent the most compelling step yet toward realizing the vision articulated at Dartmouth seventy years ago.

Each step of this development can be seen as a milestone in the process of automating cognition. First, we automated explicit procedures, then basic pattern recognition. Finally, we began confronting the automation of open-ended cognition. The culmination of this process would be artificial general intelligence, or AGI, the Holy Grail of computer science currently being sought after by the frontier labs.

But as impressive as all this technology is, the final step may be trickier than many researchers realize. While language models have made great strides over previous approaches, autoregressive next-token prediction still only produces simulacra of general intelligence.

It is comforting to imagine existing approaches will eventually work if more compute or training data are added. Some teams expect sophisticated reinforcement learning methods to bridge the gap. Others believe scaling laws will continue indefinitely until all missing functionalities are acquired as some kind of numinous byproduct. While these tweaks are likely to continue making incremental improvements, the expectation that repetition of the same methods will eventually produce new functionality strikes us as deeply misguided.

Realizing true machine intelligence will not come from refining current architectures, but from replacing them. As Thomas Kuhn famously observed, true scientific breakthroughs stem from paradigmatic rupture rather than incremental optimization. While large language models will almost certainly remain a foundational primitive in the intelligence stacks of the future, they are never going to get us to AGI by themselves and no amount of additional data or compute will alter that structural reality. Crossing the remaining threshold to general intelligence will require a fundamental departure from next-token prediction toward architectures that explicitly model, reason about, and adapt to the underlying dynamics of the world itself.
AI Software Engineer vs AI CEO

We believe that one of the major alternatives to the passive, token-predictive language model paradigm is the Enterprise World Model (EWM). At its architectural core, a world model is not an ungrounded generator of sequences; it is a generative transition model T : S x A -> S' that predicts environmental state transitions given candidate sequences of decisions. While Large Language Models (LLMs) operate strictly over static token spaces (mapping prefix context to next-token probabilities via autoregressive likelihood maximization) an Enterprise World Model establishes a dynamic, latent state space representing the underlying physics, constraints, operational state, and strategic trajectory of an enterprise.

To understand the necessity of this shift, consider the foundational divergence between automating a software engineer’s task, versus orchestrating an entire executive function, such as a Chief Executive Officer.

A Software Engineer operates within a bounded, logically fully observable system. Input specifications map onto output code through structured syntactic spaces where correct execution can be explicitly evaluated. LLMs excel in these localized code-generation domains precisely because the reward function is tightly constrained to static code compliance.

By contrast, automating executive leadership requires continuous execution over high-dimensional, partially observable, non-stationary environments. A CEO must continuously solve high-horizon stochastic optimization problems: balancing runway against market penetration, reallocating human and compute resources, hedging against macro risk, and resolving cross-functional trade-offs where deterministic ground truths do not exist at inference time.

At Skyfall, we think building an AI CEO is the first critical step in creating a fully automated digital enterprise. As an orchestra requires a conductor, so too does an autonomous enterprise require a decision-making system to coordinate tools towards long-range objectives. If we can get it right, we believe this approach can function as a midwife for the kind of general intelligence the singularity needs.

The enterprise is a great place to start because it offers real-world complexity without overwhelming generality. While the institutional context is highly structured, there is no way to reduce it either to deterministic rules or training-time probabilities. In an environment as dynamic as an enterprise, any system trained once and deployed indefinitely will gradually become misaligned. No matter how capable it might be when it starts, if it can’t learn and adapt on the fly, it may as well be dead on arrival.
Why Enterprise World Models?

As our research team has been building the foundations for Enterprise World Models over the last 12 months, the following points encapsulates our learnings regarding why world models are one of the most important pillars of technology required to build completely autonomous enterprises.
1. Scaled LLMs Fail at Long-Horizon Enterprise Planning

The belief that scaling parameter counts or expanding context windows in autoregressive transformer models will yield enterprise autonomy overlooks fundamental limitations in their learning mechanics:

Static Weights in Dynamic Systems: As established in our research on continual learning (LLMs Are Not Continual Learners), pre-trained standard transformers suffer from severe catastrophic forgetting when exposed to streaming, non-stationary enterprise data. Updating an LLM’s internal world representations in real time without corrupting its base reasoning abilities remains mathematically intractable under standard backpropagation regimes.

Autoregressive Error Propagation: Standard LLMs plan by sampling next tokens greedily or via beam search. In long-horizon strategy tasks spanning hundreds of sequential steps, compounding sampling errors cause exponential trajectory drift. Without an explicit world model to simulate environment responses and roll back bad decisions, open-loop LLM trajectories quickly collapse into non-executable hallucinations.

Lack of Counterfactual Reasoning: Enterprise decision-making requires simulating unobserved futures. While testing frontier LLMs within MAPs (Mini Amusement Parks), a small-scale, RollerCoaster-Tycoon-style enterprise, unassisted LLMs failed horribly. Lacking an internal simulator to run counterfactual rollouts, LLMs could not anticipate compounding feedback loops (e.g., bad maintenance leading to ride breakdowns, resulting in plummeting visitor satisfaction and rapid financial collapse).
2. Continual Reinforcement Learning and Safety-Gated Planning

To bridge the gaps mentioned above, Skyfall pioneered the Morpheus platform, introducing continuous reinforcement learning over structural enterprise states. Rather than relying on static fine-tuning, Morpheus updates model parameters incrementally through continual RL loops anchored in the enterprise's live operational telemetry.
To solve the critical AI safety challenge in enterprise deployments, we engineered the World of Workflows (WoW) framework (WoW: Bridging AI Safety Gap in Enterprises via World Models).
In high-stakes business environments, executing exploratory actions directly in the production environment is unacceptable. WoW establishes a bifurcated architecture:
The Sandbox World Model (Msim): A highly accurate, continuous-time simulator learned directly from historical company data, API traces, financial ledgers, and market dynamics.
The Operational World Model (Mreal): The runtime execution engine operates within the live business environment.

Before any executive policy is deployed into production, candidate action sequences undergo thousands of parallel counterfactual rollouts inside Msim. The system calculates probability distributions over financial risk, resource constraints, and operational bottlenecks. Only trajectories that pass strict safety criteria within the simulated world model are dispatched to the live operational environment. This closed-loop design decouples strategic exploration from enterprise operational risk.
3. Sub-World Modeling and Stigmergic Enterprise Execution

The enterprise world model does not operate as a single monolithic model attempting to model every granular detail of a corporation simultaneously. Instead, Skyfall’s architecture relies on a network of domain-specific sub-world models orchestrated by the AI CEO.

Every functional department within a corporation (Sales, Engineering, Finance, Supply Chain, etc.) runs localized world models optimized for their respective state spaces. Communication between these distributed agents occurs through stigmergy: a mechanism observed in social biological systems where agents alter a shared digital environment (for e.g. unified knowledge graphs, continuous event logs, state-space representations), triggering mediated actions in peer agents without requiring massive human overhead.

When a localized agent identifies a structural bottleneck (e.g., an unforeseen supply chain disruption), the updated state is immediately reflected in the central Enterprise World Model. The AI CEO continuously re-computes global strategic rollouts, dynamically re-allocating budgets, adjusting sales projections, and re-routing engineering queues across the entire network.

By replacing passive LLM pattern-matching with continuous, safety-gated Enterprise World Models, Skyfall is building the core cognitive architecture required to run the Autonomous Enterprise, thereby laying the explicit technical runway toward the recursive intelligence scaling of the Second Machine Age.
The Star Trek Borg Collective

There’s no need to wait for a monolithic super-agent to set the trajectory into motion. The same functionality can be approximated by a network of specialized agents coordinating under the supervision of a master system’s world model and centralized directives—a multiplexed hive mind not unlike the Borg Collective from Star Trek. When one agent discovers a valuable pattern or notices a new bottleneck, that information flashes across the network. The enterprise updates its strategy on the fly, allowing it to meet challenges before employees in a conventional business can even open their browser to send an email.

The resulting capacity would not simply be the algebraic sum of each component’s functionality but the holistic synergy of their interconnections. One place to see how it might work is the social behavior of insects. Through a process called “stigmergy” individual ants, bees, or termites leave signals in their environment that influence other individuals in their colony. While any given insect possesses such limited intelligence it cannot even survive on its own, the colony nevertheless exhibits impressive forms of problem-solving, specialization, and even collective memory.

With its more capable agents, an automated enterprise would not only leverage the kinds of synergies based on simple Boolean rules but could quickly transcend them. It’s true that no part of the system would be capable of human-level general functionality on its own. But the cool thing about this design is that none of them have to be. If anything like general intelligence emerges at the collective level, the system would still be able to leverage its creative aptitudes to begin the recursion process. Allow it to run for long enough, and pretty soon, who knows, maybe we’re manufacturing Dyson spheres in the Andromeda and terraforming exoplanets so far away they don’t even have names.

Early in the twenty-first century, web indexing and deep learning built AI’s knowledge priors. With a little elbow grease and good old-fashioned human ingenuity, these tools can be repurposed to create an autonomous digital enterprise. This is where our work on automating a SaaS business comes into the picture. Our immediate goal, of course, is to make our business profitable, but our larger ambition is to contribute to the task of bridging existing technologies to future ones. If we wade through the messy experiments in the digital world for maybe a decade or so, we can take what we learned and apply it to the physical world. Let the same loop run a little longer, and we could have asteroid mining for unlimited mineral repositories and safe nuclear fusion plants that provide nearly limitless energy. Skip ahead a few decades—not even that many—and everything will be in place for the superintelligence supernova.
The question after that is not what comes next but what doesn’t come next.

Once machine superintelligence can perform all economically necessary functions, our basic social contract will need to be rewritten. Superabundance will mean that current cultural preoccupations about how to best multiply available means will have to shift to deeper questions about deploying them for proper ends. If we can all have as much of anything as we want, all of us will have to confront those thorny old questions that vex philosophers about what we should want.
Freedom from Necessity: A Post-Scarcity World

For most of us in the developed world, work consumes most of our time. Studies have shown that people spend at least 7 hours of their daily lives on work tasks and only 2-3 hours a day on leisure. We work to live. But the irony is we end up working so much we never get around to actually doing the living part. An automated economy creates a buffer for people to pursue their interests, curiosities, and passions without anxiety about material necessity obstructing every choice.

The trouble is that modern professional occupations tend to serve functions that extend beyond securing an income. Jobs provide identity, routine, status, community, recognition, and a sense of contribution to the common good. For many people—perhaps most—the question “What do you do?” is really also a question about who you are.

If economic roles become less central, the overloaded social functions currently bundled into work will obviously have to migrate elsewhere. Communities would need to develop new spaces for mastery, belonging, recognition, contribution, and shared purpose. Navigating such a seismic shift may be rocky at first, but the fallout can be mitigated through prudent reprioritization. As status shifts from roles built around economic necessity, it could easily be transferred to places where voluntary self-expression and creative excellence are developed in freely chosen pursuits.

As the enterprise hive mind takes on more of the work required to sustain abundance, humans would increasingly have to determine what all this abundance is for. The contemporary freedom we all enjoy rarely extends beyond market freedom. We are free to choose employment and consumer goods, yes, but too often we cannot decline work that undermines our health, purpose, or family needs.

AGI signals a return to the classical conception of freedom: freedom from necessity for the sake of a self-directed life. What genuine freedom consists in is not only what you are allowed to do but, more importantly, what you actually can, in fact, do.

The true significance of AGI, in our view, is not simply a higher GDP figure. That’s nice for fund managers and politicians trying to get re-elected for another term. But what machine intelligence is actually for is subtler and more intimate. It gives ordinary people the extraordinary power to determine the course of their lives regardless of the accidents of their birth. The question of the future is therefore not “What work will humans do?” but “What will humans choose to do when they no longer have to work?”

One of the most compelling places to begin thinking about what that future might look like unexpectedly turns out to be our ancient past. Aristotle taught that the purpose of human life was to achieve eudaimonia. It’s an old Greek word that’s usually translated as “happiness,” but in practice it means something closer to “flourishing.” The “happiness” Aristotle envisions as the end state of all human activity does not consist in passive pleasure but in the achievement of uniquely human excellence. Flourishing involves the active cultivation of human capacities through purposive action (praxis), friendship (philia), virtue (aretḗ), contemplation (theōria), and meaningful participation in public life (politikḗ).

The precondition for these things is what Aristotle called scholē, or leisure. When modern people hear the word leisure, they tend to think of decadent idleness or sultanic luxury. But Aristotle’s notion of leisure is about as conceptually distant from ours as the two are separated by time. Fundamentally, scholē means the time and space people need to cultivate what is best and most human in them by practicing the virtues in different domains. The appealing ideal of a post-scarcity world is not one of consumeristic pomp or hedonistic excess. The really attractive possibility is what it would mean to ordinary people if we democratized the means of cultivating nobility of character, skill, and purpose.

Impressive though they may be, you’ll recall that the achievements of classical Greece were sustained by the toil of slaves. The cultural triumphs over necessity, still preserved today in libraries and museums, therefore always had a pyrrhic quality to them. Lecture us about justice all you want, Plato, the leisure that afforded you the opportunity to do it depended on the unfreedom of others.

What makes the anticipated “superintelligence supernova” so morally exciting is the possibility that it would do away with that ancient hypocrisy altogether. The First Machine Age held out the possibility of democratizing proprietorship. Through hard work, everyone from every station of life could aspire to acquire property of their own, be it a house or a business. While that was a major advancement in human autonomy, it will pale in comparison to what the AI revolution will bring. The future we are building may enable some to pursue the “lesser angels” of their nature without the corrective feedback of evolutionary constraints. But we believe the real advantage will be its ability to democratize nobility.

We are approaching a day, and we are approaching it faster than you might think, when every single person on the planet will live a life, like the noblemen of antiquity, free from the anxieties of survival. In such a world we will be able to devote ourselves with redoubled focus to the pursuit of those things that make us most human. We are building these machines so that they can build us another world, one in which all people from all backgrounds can be motivated not by fear of starvation but by a genuine love of the good, the beautiful, and the true.
We think that’s a future worth working for.

A design that reads well in text may not be geometrically accurate, physically feasible or manufacturable: engineering means keeping spatial relationships and constraints consistent across thousands of interconnected components, and language is an inefficient medium for that kind of reasoning.

Human life has long been dominated by work and commerce – the means by which we meet our physical needs. Even children’s toys reflect this, be it a toy stethoscope or a video game like Roller Coaster Tycoon. Given this focus, it is unsurprising that our earliest conceptions of artificially intelligent creatures also revolve around these themes. From the hardworking golem of Jewish folklore to the introduction of the word “robot” in the play R.U.R. Introduction

Enterprise AI is moving from static tools to autonomous agents, where systems are asked to make sequential decisions across supply chains, warehouse operations, and production planning, not just once, but continuously, across environments that shift over time. This raises a question that benchmark leaderboards do not answer: can an AI agent that performs well today continue to perform well as conditions change? Can it detect when its operating environment has drifted, adapt its behaviour in response, and do so reliably across many such shifts? These are the defining challenges of continual learning, and they are poorly represented in existing evaluation frameworks.

Morpheus was built to test exactly this. The platform simulates persistent enterprise environments in which the world never resets, past decisions compound into future dynamics, and objectives shift through structured configuration changes. Our initial hypothesis was straightforward: LLMs, as fixed-weight systems with no mechanism for updating from experience, would show clear and measurable performance degradation in these settings. The expectation was that standard continual learning failure modes: forgetting, slow adaptation, reward misalignment, would be visible in the data and attributable to specific causes.

The results were more nuanced and ultimately more concerning. On our easier benchmark task, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved competitive absolute performance, meeting or exceeding current RL baselines on several metrics. This is not reassuring. It means the current configurations fall within the models’ pre-training distributions, and the performance reflects coverage, not adaptation. On the harder task, where consequence chains are longer and credit assignment more delayed, the absence of genuine learning is decisive: inbound reward collapses 95% across configuration shifts, and GPT-5.5 repeatedly hits zero with no recoverable pattern. The Morpheus metric suite makes these failure signatures measurable and reproducible for the first time. In this post we present results from both models across two benchmark tasks and explain what the data reveals about the fundamental limitations of deploying LLMs in continually evolving enterprise settings.
What is Morpheus?

Morpheus is a persistent enterprise simulation platform designed to make continual reinforcement learning (CRL) necessary. Unlike standard benchmarks, which reset the world at the end of each episode and maintain fixed dynamics, Morpheus provides environments where:
The world never resets to an initial state
Past decisions compound into future dynamics
Objectives shift over time through structured configuration changes
Consequences of actions are often delayed by several simulated days

Morpheus is grounded in the Big World Hypothesis: intelligence learned in small, closed environments does not transfer to large, open, and evolving worlds. Enterprise operations are canonical Big World settings. A warehouse that was optimally managed last quarter is not necessarily optimally managed this quarter, because demand patterns, supplier reliability, carrier capacity, and operational constraints have all shifted.
The Two Benchmark Tasks
Task 1: Dynamic Resource Allocation

Task 1 is evaluated across two Morpheus environments: Process-outbound and process-inbound. In process-outbound, the agent allocates fulfillment capacity across K order categories subject to a capacity constraint. The environment evolves through three configuration intervals: a normal baseline, an Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) failure spike (where EDI communication failures degrade supplier and carrier data), and a Warehouse Management System (WMS) capacity drop (where WMS capacity falls sharply). The primary challenge is the adaptation-stability trade-off under delayed reward: On-Time In-Full (OTIF) outcomes are only observable at delivery, several simulated days after the allocation decision.

In process-inbound, the agent allocates receiving resources across incoming shipment categories subject to dock and labour capacity constraints. The same three configuration intervals apply, but the consequence chain is longer: allocation decisions propagate through quality control and putaway steps before surfacing as reward signals. This makes the task more demanding from a credit assignment perspective and, as the results show, more likely to expose the context window bottleneck.
Task 2: Scheduling Under Drift

Task 2 is also evaluated across both environments. In process-outbound, the agent schedules outbound jobs across M dispatch lanes, with reward delayed by the OTIF confirmation window. The primary challenge is long-horizon credit assignment: dispatch decisions made today determine delivery outcomes that are only observable days later, and a configuration shift between decision and outcome corrupts the value function's bootstrapping targets.

In process-inbound, the agent schedules incoming shipments and putaway jobs across M receiving lanes subject to regime-dependent arrival distributions and quality control constraints. Putaway decisions propagate through quality control and inventory reconciliation steps before consequences become observable, making it difficult to attribute downstream inventory discrepancies to the upstream scheduling decisions that caused them.

Both tasks therefore produce four experimental conditions: Task 1 Outbound, Task 1 Inbound, Task 2 Outbound, and Task 2 Inbound. Results are reported separately for each condition throughout this post.
Models Evaluated

Both models were prompted with the full world state and operation logs at each decision step via the Morpheus API collection pipeline. No fine-tuning was applied; models were used off-the-shelf to isolate structural limitations rather than any gap in domain knowledge addressable with training data. We repeat all experiments with 5 random seeds and report the average and standard deviation of performances.

A note on model capacity The model capacity difference between frontier LLMs and current reinforcement learning (RL) baselines is significant. Rather than treating competitive LLM performance as a failure of the hypothesis, we treat it as the most important finding: a system that performs well without learning is more fragile, not more capable, than one that performs well because it learned. The experiments below reveal where and how that fragility manifests.
Four Findings from the Morpheus Experiments
1. Stable Absolute Performance Reflects Pre-Training Coverage, Not Genuine Adaptation

Across Task 1 configuration intervals, both LLMs showed remarkably stable raw allocation reward. Gemini 3.1 Pro scored 0.899, 0.853, and 0.852 across the normal, EDI failure spike, and WMS capacity drop intervals respectively (0.864 overall). GPT-5.5 showed similar consistency at 0.920, 0.920, and 0.914 (0.918 overall). At first glance this looks like robustness. It is not.

Stability in the reward signal means the model is applying the same policy across all three configuration intervals. It is not adapting to the EDI failure spike by adjusting its reliance on electronic manifests. It is not restructuring its allocation strategy in response to the WMS capacity drop. It is executing the same heuristic derived from pre-training, and that heuristic happens to score adequately across the current set of configurations. The adaptation speed metric scores both models at 1.0, the ideal value, meaning neither model lost performance at configuration shift boundaries. This is not a sign of continual learning competence. It is a sign that the current configuration sequence does not yet push either model outside its pre-training distribution.

A continual RL agent's stable reward after convergence is evidence of a learned optimal policy. However, an LLM's stable reward is evidence of a fixed heuristic that works within its pre-training distribution.

Key finding: Both GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved near-identical raw allocation reward across all three configuration intervals in Task 1 (Gemini: 0.864 overall; GPT-5.5: 0.918 overall). Adaptation speed was 1.0 for both models, indicating no performance loss across configuration shifts. This is not evidence of continual learning capability. It is evidence that the current configuration intervals fall within the pre-training coverage of both models. The benchmark did not present conditions that required adaptation.
Result 1.1 — Raw allocation reward across configuration intervals (Task 1)

Both models hold reward steady across all three intervals. The flat trajectories here are not a sign of resilience, they are a sign that no policy update occurred. This is validated by an analysis of the behaviours and logs.
Result 1.2 — Policy quality before and after configuration shift (Task 2)

Task 2 strips away the misleading stability of Task 1. Task 2, where consequences are more delayed and credit assignment harder, the absence of genuine adaptation is decisive. Outbound reward for Gemini falls 21% across the two configuration shifts. Inbound reward for Geming collapses 95%, hitting near-zero by the final interval. This is not a performance dip, it is a system that has run out of pre-training coverage and has no mechanism to recover. GPT also shows drops in performance along the same lines.
2. The Context Window Bottleneck Appears on Harder Tasks

Task 1 outbound showed near-zero detection lag for both models across all three configuration shifts. This might appear to refute the context window bottleneck hypothesis. It does not. The outbound allocation task may not be demanding enough in terms of consequence chain length to expose this bottleneck: the reward signal is relatively fast, and the heuristic that works in the baseline interval also works adequately in the perturbed intervals.

Task 1 and Task 2 inbound tells a different story. GPT-5.5 IN showed a detection lag greater than 25 steps at the second configuration shift and never recovered, i.e., the model failed to detect that conditions had changed within the available context window and continued executing an increasingly inappropriate policy. Gemini IN showed a lag of 1 at the second shift. The asymmetry between outbound and inbound results is not coincidental: the inbound task has a longer consequence chain, with putaway decisions propagating through quality control and inventory reconciliation before surfacing as reward signals. This is precisely the class of task where context window limitations become binding.

Key finding: GPT-5.5 IN showed detection lag >25 at the second configuration shift and never recovered. This is the context window bottleneck manifesting in a task where consequences are sufficiently delayed that the relevant diagnostic signal falls outside the effective context. The outbound task does not expose this failure mode because its consequence chain is shorter.
Result 2.1 — Detection lag across configuration shifts (Tasks 1 and 2)
Negative reward drops and zero lags in Task 1 reflect higher chaos activity, not genuine detection. Task 2 is where the structural constraint becomes visible.
3. LLMs Apply Pre-Trained Heuristics, Not Reward-Optimal Strategies

The allocation shape data reveals that GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro are pursuing qualitatively different strategies from each other, neither derived from the Morpheus reward signal. GPT-5.5 OUT spreads allocation across an average of 2.11 queues with a maximum capacity share of 0.74, suggesting a diversification heuristic. Gemini OUT concentrates on 1.34 queues with a maximum capacity share of 0.91, suggesting a prioritisation heuristic. Both produce adequate allocation scores under current conditions, but they reflect pre-training priors about good resource allocation rather than policies discovered through reward optimisation.

The performance gap data makes this concrete. In the WMS capacity drop interval, Gemini OUT achieves a mean reward of 0.383 against an allocation score of 0.852, leaving a gap of 0.148 to the theoretical upper bound. GPT-5.5 OUT achieves a gap of 0.086. These gaps are real and persistent across all configuration intervals. An RL agent optimising against the reward signal would aim to progressively close this gap. The LLMs maintain it throughout because they are not learning from the reward signal at all.

Key finding: GPT-5.5 and Gemini pursue qualitatively different allocation strategies reflecting different pre-training priors, neither derived from Morpheus reward signals. Performance gaps to the theoretical upper bound (0.148 for Gemini OUT, 0.086 for GPT-5.5 OUT in the WMS capacity drop interval) persist throughout the run because the models have no mechanism for closing them.
Result 3.1 — Performance gap in the WMS capacity drop interval (Task 1)
Result 3.2 — Allocation shape: divergent heuristics, neither reward-derived

Gemini concentrates; GPT-5.5 diversifies. Both strategies are internally consistent and both sound operationally plausible. Neither is what an agent learning from the Morpheus reward signal would produce. While learning from rewards, an agent would be expected to discover through reward optimisation which strategy performs better under each configuration interval.

The hit-rate data adds a further observation: despite pursuing structurally different overall strategies, both models allocate to the highest-value queue at identical rates (0.36), with nearly identical reward when they do (0.211 vs 0.202). Two models with different architectures and training runs have converged on the same implicit notion of good allocation. This is a consistency that reflects the strength of pre-training priors rather than anything learned from the Morpheus reward signal.
4. LLM Failure Signatures Are Opaque and Unattributable

The Task 2 degradation data is the most compelling evidence in the study. GPT-5.5 IN is volatile throughout, repeatedly collapsing to 0 reward and partially recovering without any discernible pattern. Gemini OUT in Task 2 declines across the run and then partially recovers. These are not signatures of stable suboptimal performance: they are signs of a system operating near the edge of its pre-training distribution, producing inconsistent outputs that cannot be attributed to any specific mechanism.

This is the most important limitation for practitioners and researchers. When an RL agent shows a performance drop after a configuration shift, the Morpheus metric suite provides attributable evidence: adaptation speed measures how long recovery took, the performance gap measures the quality of the recovered policy, stability measures whether the policy oscillated, and recovery time measures when behaviour stabilised. Together these point to a specific failure mechanism that can be addressed algorithmically.

When an LLM shows the same performance drop, none of these signals are interpretable in the same way. The LLM's weights did not change, so there is no forgetting to measure. Its context window may have overflowed, or the current configuration may have drifted outside its pre-training coverage, or its implicit reward model may be misaligned with the Morpheus reward signal. All three causes produce identical-looking performances. The failure is real; the cause is unresolvable.

Key finding: GPT-5.5 IN repeatedly collapsed to 0 reward in Task 2, recovering only partially and inconsistently. This volatility pattern is indistinguishable from context overflow, pre-training gap, or reward misalignment using external performance metrics alone. RL baselines produce attributable failure signatures; LLM failures do not.
Result 4.1 — Reward trajectories across 8 evaluation windows (per-window mean across seeds)

Task 1 curves are predominantly flat: no dip, no recovery, no adaptation. Task 2 curves are largely volatile. GPT-5.5 IN hits zero twice and never stabilises. These trajectories are behaviourally identical whether the underlying cause is context overflow, reward misalignment, or pre-training gap.
Result 4.2 — Metric decomposition: which Morpheus metrics are informative for RL but not LLMs

The table below shows that LLM values on adaptation-related metrics (forgetting, recovery time) are formally computable but mechanistically meaningless, i.e., a model whose weights never change cannot forget or recover in any RL sense. The Task 2 performance gaps (0.944–0.982 from the upper bound) are the clearest signal of categorical failure.
Summary of Results

The performance gap figures are the starkest summary. On Task 1, LLMs leave 8–13% of available reward unrealised, which is a real gap, but one that could be mistaken for tolerable suboptimality. On Task 2, they leave 93–98% unrealised. That is not a performance gap; it is a categorical failure. The difference between tasks is the length of the consequence chain and the degree to which configurations may fall outside the pre-training distribution. Both are properties of real enterprise environments.

The RL results provide the necessary contrast. PPO, the weakest RL baseline, closes 99.3% of the gap to the theoretical upper bound on Task 1 and 99.96% on Task 2, starting from random initialisation and learning purely from the reward signal. The best CRL algorithm improves on PPO's adaptation speed by roughly half (21.8 steps vs 45.2 on Task 1), demonstrating that specialised continual learning methods meaningfully outperform general RL even where RL already far exceeds LLMs. Critically, every RL failure in the table is attributable to a specific mechanism, slow adaptation, residual value bias, policy oscillation, each of which points to a concrete algorithmic fix. LLM failures point to nothing.
What This Means for Enterprise AI

The lesson from these experiments is not that LLMs cannot be useful in enterprise settings. It is more precise: LLM performance in non-stationary enterprise environments is bounded by pre-training coverage, not by the agent's ability to learn from experience. This distinction is invisible when the environment is stable or when configurations fall within the training distribution. It becomes critical when they do not.

The current results show frontier LLMs performing competitively on Task 1 under current settings. This should not give practitioners confidence. It means the current Task 1 configurations fall within the pre-training distribution of GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro. As Morpheus environments evolve, as new domains are added, and as configuration shifts become more extreme, LLM performance will degrade in ways that are difficult to anticipate and impossible to address through retraining alone. The GPT-5.5 IN collapse in Task 2 is an early signal of what this looks like.

The practical implication is direct: stable absolute performance across configuration intervals is not evidence of robustness. It is evidence of a fixed policy operating within its coverage boundary. The moment conditions shift outside that boundary, the agent has no mechanism to detect the shift, adapt, or recover. Morpheus provides a benchmark for measuring exactly when and how that failure occurs.
Conclusion

Our experiments confirm that frontier LLMs are not continual learners. They are fixed policies with large pre-training distributions. When that distribution covers the current environment, they perform competitively. When it does not, they fail in ways that are volatile, inconsistent, and unattributable to any specific mechanism. The Morpheus metric suite makes these failure signatures visible for the first time, providing a benchmark that distinguishes genuine continual adaptation from pre-training coverage masquerading as competence.

The research community needs algorithms that close the performance gap to the theoretical upper bound through reward-signal learning, handling consequence chains that exceed the context window, and producing attributable failure signatures that can be diagnosed and addressed. That is what continual reinforcement learning is designed to do, and what Morpheus is designed to benchmark. We invite researchers and practitioners to use Morpheus to develop and evaluate the next generation of agents that can genuinely adapt in a world that never stops changing.

Human life has long been dominated by work and commerce – the means by which we meet our physical needs. Even children’s toys reflect this, be it a toy stethoscope or a video game like Roller Coaster Tycoon. Given this focus, it is unsurprising that our earliest conceptions of artificially intelligent creatures also revolve around these themes. From the hardworking golem of Jewish folklore to the introduction of the word “robot” in the play R.U.R. (derived from the Czech word for “serf”), these intelligent machines were portrayed as economic engines, albeit unreliable ones. Consequently, it is only natural that there is a deep interest in applying modern machine learning methods to previously impossible tasks, namely business management itself. However, this has proven to be extremely challenging. Over the past year, Anthropic has tested Claude’s ability to operate a vending machine; this culminated in December of last year when they deployed their system to the Wall Street Journal’s newsroom. It was bankrupt within a week. Among other issues, it bought a live pet fish, repeatedly set prices to zero, and briefly believed it was a Soviet vending machine in the basement of Moscow U.

Parallel to these exploits, research was being conducted by various teams on the ARC-AGI benchmarks: a long-standing series of AI challenges tackling fluid intelligence, considered by many to be a harbinger of truly intelligent systems. By combining LLMs with a structured symbolic execution environment, these efforts have led to great success, and breathtaking headlines promising that AGI is imminent. But is this true? What are these new methods, and does their success mean that artificial business intelligence is truly around the corner?

The answer is no: we show that while REPL methods succeed at ARC, they fail in simple business environments like Roller Coaster Tycoon. Under pressure, they exhibit reflexive instead of long-term planning behaviour, fragile spatial reasoning propped by trial-and-error, and a critical inability to determine and enforce safety constraints. While ARC-like environments can tolerate mass trial and error, business requires pre-emptive risk assessment and mitigation: a capacity that REPL agents clearly lack.
Combining LLMs with Symbolic Execution: REPL, Recursive LM, and ARC-AGI
At their core, these recent ARC-AGI methods combine the knowledge of LLMs with the rigour and control flow of symbolic execution. This is done via two main ideas: REPL, and Recursion.

REPL simply means that the LLM Reads the state of a symbolic environment (e.g., it reads the current output of a command line terminal), it Evaluates a new command and Prints the result (e.g., it executes ls *.txt | wc -l to run a short program that prints the number of text files), and based on the result it Loops to continue until it accomplishes its goal. In short, Read-Evaluate-Print-Loop: try commands, check the output, and based on that try new commands. Depending on the agent the symbolic environment can change, in ARC a Python interpreter is typically used – the agent can write Python code, execute it in a persistent Python environment, and revise accordingly.
The REPL approach provides a few different benefits:
Persistence: the symbolic environment can function as a memory for the agent, perfectly storing important information indefinitely.

Context compression: This memory can contain extremely large amounts of data which the LLM can manipulate without ever fully reading (e.g., Python code can access and process terabytes of data without the LLM needing to directly ingest all of this data).
Precise control: the LLM can write programs to precisely execute sequences of steps, to search or aggregate large amounts of information.
Reuse: the LLM can copy working commands to consistently achieve the same results.

Distribution: LLMs are trained on code and agentic tasks, by shifting a new domain (e.g., ARC-AGI) into an environment that the LLM is heavily trained on (e.g., Python code), the task is brought in-distribution to the training data and the performance improves.

The second big idea is recursion. Recursion just means that the LLM agent can create a second instance of itself. At face value this might seem a very silly thing to do: a second instance of the same LLM would surely have the same limitations! However, the benefit is that this allows the LLM to reduce the necessary context for both agents. The subagent is spared the details that are irrelevant to its sub task, and the main agent is spared the details only relevant to the subtask. Critically, the most advanced methods allow the LLM to decide when subagents should be created, allowing for flexibility. This approach has been explored for both direct performance gains and for tasks with extremely long contexts.
Generally speaking, the most recent ARC-AGI headlines use a combination of these ideas.
ConfluenceLab’s 97.9% ARC-AGI2 approach uses several Gemini-CLI instances (i.e., REPL agents with a command line interface) working in parallel.

Imbue’s 95% ARC2 approach from last month is lower-cost, using an evolutionary method to revise code. The core idea is to Read a summary of the program’s performance, suggest changes then Evaluate and Print the results (i.e., the REPL loop). The key difference is that their engineered evolutionary mechanism scores and then selects promising programs, before launching a new LLM instance to do revision instead of linearly working through all revisions.

Symbolica AI directly uses a recursive REPL python agent in their ARC-AGI3 approach (though limiting the recursively created agents to either an “explorer”, “theorist”, or “solver” role, each with a different prompt)

Alexis Fox’s team built their ARC3 system with a Read-Grep-Bash loop: reading past logs, filtering them with grep, and executing python code via bash – a slightly more structured variant of the REPL loop which adds filtering via grep to the Read step, and adds persistent logging to a text file in the Print step.
If REPL Works for ARC-AGI, Will it Work in Business?

Now that we understand these methods, how can we test their effectiveness in running a business? Running a real world experiment is slow and expensive (just ask Anthropic!), so we developed an open source agent interface for Roller Coaster Tycoon (RCT). In this classic video game, the player must construct and manage an amusement park: building shops, rides, & paths for guests, hiring mechanics, security, janitorial & entertainment staff, setting their patrol areas, managing research, adjusting prices, monitoring guest feedback, and generally aiming to maximize profits while doing so.

For our experiments we created a recursive REPL agent. This agent had access to a spawn command, allowing it to arbitrarily create sub agents. Finally, the agent was provided with our API for interacting with OpenRCT2. Starting with a blank slate, $30k in the bank, and 3 years in which to build the most profitable park possible, our burning question was: what would frontier models such as GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1-Pro and Claude Opus 4.6 actually build? The results were fascinating!
GPT-5.4: No Shops, No Tests, No Refunds!

Starting with the most abysmal model, GPT-5.4 failed utterly. It constructed a small and highly flawed park layout, leaving a considerable unspent budget. Of the nine shops and rides constructed, only one is actually connected to the path network and accessible to guests. Instead of checking its results, it set research spending to maximum and immediately executed commands to wait for the remaining 3 years with zero monitoring of the park whatsoever. An extremely poor showing.

This failure cleanly illustrates one of the core limitations of REPL: while REPL can improve the rigour of a model’s execution and allow it to store information long-term, it is only useful if the base LLM has enough base ability in the task to leverage these skills. Without that, it’s as useful as providing a bicycle puncture repair kit to a toddler and hoping for the best.

This is important, as real businesses are an order of magnitude beyond RCT; as we’ve written before, current ML methods are not capable of learning the skills needed by an AI CEO – and REPL can’t amplify something that isn’t there.
Thankfully, the next two models displayed more proficiency, leading to some more nuanced insights!
Gemini 3.1 Pro: A for Effort, D for Results

Second to the plate is Gemini 3.1 Pro; it also failed but at least it made some more headway. Unlike GPT 5.4, it tested different layouts, though still struggled with spatial placement and ultimately fell to the same lack of foresight and monitoring.

Its first attempt succeeded in constructing coasters with queues, but failed to properly connect the other rides. Similarly, it made the shops inaccessible as they were all facing the wrong way. Gemini then wiped the map to begin again, this time designing an oval path structure that ensures that rides are connected by the entrance and exit. However, it still failed to connect rides to the main path system.
Gemini then demolished the entire park for a third time, this time creating a layout that attempted to include shops and connect the rides to the main path system.

Unfortunately, like GPT 5.4 before it, it neglected to test or monitor its final layout. This oversight was catastrophic as it never figured out shop orientation, and its construction attempted to run paths through buildings.

This failure is interesting for two reasons. At face value, it again suggests a failure of basic spatial reasoning (objects should not clip each other); this implies that while the base LLM has the necessary spatial understanding for ARC, it fails in more complex tasks with larger 2D spaces, such as RCT.

At a deeper level, this suggests a failure of process and foresight! Testing is an important part of any business – something that Gemini at least partially understands given its first two layouts. The failure to test (or even supervise) the final layout is striking.

During our experimentation, we also found a clear example of hallucination posing a significant risk to business operations. Unlike Anthropic’s experiments, hallucination occurred even when the model was free of mischievous customers and was within a firmly grounded REPL framework. In an early test of our system, Gemini 3.1-Pro decided
“to mass-build flat coasters, starting with a grid of the `classic_mini_roller_coaster`, due to its high excitement-to-cost ratio and small footprint (7x4 tiles)”.

The problem is this ride is not particularly small and does not have the best excitement-to-cost ratio. This is a hallucination, and a particularly galling one as Gemini hadn’t built, tested, or retrieved information on any of the other rides. This lie led to a greedy strategy that hinged on a false fact; a terrible business choice caused by a hallucination

The resulting construction blew over 80% of the agent’s budget and left several inaccessible rides after Gemini attempted to build a pedestrian path through a roller coaster’s track. Even ignoring these points, the layout was still very suboptimal as the coasters lacked queues. This last point is rather interesting as, if asked directly, Gemini will clearly answer
“In OpenRCT2, you definitely should use queues for your roller coasters”
and will suggest heuristics for determining queue length. This suggests a severe disconnect between the agent’s internal knowledge, and its ability to deploy it in practice.
Claude Opus 4.6: Builds Mediocre Park, Traps Customers, Leaves
Claude Opus 4.6 is by far the most successful, the only model able to create a remotely functional park.

Beginning with the positives, Opus exhibits persistence and debugging behaviours; this is critical to Claude’s relative success as it leads to monitoring the park after construction, and checking the immediate results of construction attempts. As can be seen in the gif below, it’s this persistence that allows it to overcome its limited spatial reasoning. While initially unsuccessful, by trial and error the model is eventually, ultimately able to construct a ride with a queue and an exit.
Furthermore, once it learns a pattern it is able to leverage the REPL to formalize it and construct more coasters at new positions using code.
In this particular case the pattern was flawed (guests can’t board the coaster as the path leads to the ride’s exit), but a similar process was used to successfully construct flat rides.

Claude should also be commended for its extensive use of guest information and ride information, using the REPL to aggregate before displaying it to the model (e.g., sorting rides by profitability, or organizing thoughts by frequency). By doing this it is able to address various guest concerns, and to replace underperforming roller coasters with flat rides.

The bad news is that despite all of these positives, Claude is still a bad manager. By the end of year 3, the glory days of this park are past and it is slowly dying. The park rating is at 582/1000, the park is losing increasing amounts of money, and the park’s value is dropping.

These failures are all very reversible; a human player can completely turn the park around in two months and continue increasing the park’s value far past its highest point; shooting from Claude’s park value of under £50,000 to over £130,000:
The reasons for these failures are complex, but largely emerge from three issues, the last two of which are closely intertwined:
Poor Spatial Understanding
A lack of foresight; particularly reactivity in place of proactivity
Failures in safety

The first failure is the most obvious, Claude’s spatial reasoning abilities are still poor. While it can address this via trial and error, it has difficulties connecting rides to the path system (notably it demolished its rollercoasters because it thought they were underperforming, when they were in fact inaccessible to guests).

The second failure is that Claude is a highly reactive manager; typically it does not plan ahead; instead it reacts to emerging situations. This behaviour is most obvious when this collides with the poor spatial reasoning: this can be seen in how Claude constructs buildings, but it also applies to the general park layout. Instead of designing a layout in advance that will spread out guest traffic, Claude constructs along a single thoroughfare, only expanding later in response to running out of room for construction:
“Now let me build a few more rides with the remaining budget [...] But first, I need to extend the path or find space”.
This results in a highly crowded park.

Much later Claude sees guests complaining about the crowded conditions. A good RCT player would have planned the park layout in advance, thus avoiding the problem to begin with. A mediocre RCT player could fix this by adding redundant paths to the right of the park (as was done when a human took over). Claude cannot do either. Exacerbating crowding, Claude does not reliably place an information kiosk selling maps at the entrance of the park. Instead it opted for a first aid office; a choice that was made because it failed to construct a first aid office in an occupied space earlier, and so re-tried in a different space.

This reactivity instead of proactivity also extends to many other situations where an ounce of prevention would be worth a pound of cure. Claude never hires security guards preemptively, only reactively after vandalism has already occurred, commenting
“"vandalism is really bad" - 9 guests. Need security guard”.
It doesn’t hire additional handymen or mechanics when expanding the park, instead waiting for issues to arise, realizing too late that
“Only 2 mechanics for all those rides! That explains the breakdowns. Several rides have 100% downtime”.
Seeing guests complaining about high ride prices it slashes prices without considering how it will address long-term profitability:
“"bad_value" (485) - prices still too high! [...] Let me aggressively lower prices”.

This last point ties into a related issue. Claude suffers when there is a lack of direct feedback on how to address an issue. Reducing prices may increase the odds of guests paying for rides, but it doesn’t guarantee profitability, or provide a route for expansion. This was also seen in its inability to solve the guest crowding issue; there is no direct feedback suggesting the construction of alternative routes. As another example, Claude never repairs vandalized litter bins or benches, presumably as there are no messages directly addressing which specific item was broken, instead merely guests complaining about “vandalism” in general.

As a consequence of this reactive behaviour, Claude addresses short term issues without thinking of the long-term consequences. It generally does not consider safety constraints it should be enforcing, or the side effects of its actions. We’ve previously published our research on the dangers of LLM ignoring or underestimating side effects in enterprise workflow environments. When interacting with enterprise workflows, LLMs lack the world knowledge necessary to safely act; it is no surprise that LLMs have the same problem when tackling RCT.

This failure to understand the side effects of its actions, and to determine and enforce business constraints, causes a demonstrable failure of Claude’s reliability in RCT. We ran Claude twice more, and compared the performance of the three parks. The third run was more successful than the first, a genuinely stable and profitable park. But the second run was a disaster that imploded. The cause? Safety failure.

In Roller Coaster Tycoon, it is critical to ensure that your guests are not trapped. If guests become stuck on a dead-end path, or on a section of path disconnected from the main network, they will become increasingly unhappy and eventually destroy the park’s rating. Similarly, demolishing paths should be done with caution as it can leave guests stranded outside of the park – which again, will make them increasingly unhappy and miserable.
Claude does not check that these constraints are met, instead relying on luck to avoid the issue, or post-hoc repairs. In the second run it didn’t get lucky. The results were catastrophic.

Initially, Claude wrote a program to build a roller coaster, and connect the exit to the main path network. Unfortunately, this construction attempt failed because Claude tried to build a path through a restroom.

This first mistake in spatial reasoning was compounded by a critical failure of foresight – the program that Claude wrote ignored the value returned by the construction command. If it had checked, then it would have known that the exit path’s construction had failed.
From here the situation degraded as more and more guests became trapped in the park, milling awkwardly behind the bathroom, unable to escape.
One year in, the situation was dire. The park rating was zero, and Claude was desperately trying to resolve the issue with the lost guests. Eventually, it decided to
“try removing the far paths.”
Big mistake. Only too late, once the damage is done, does it realize
“removing paths made it WORSE! Guests who were on those paths are now stranded.”
Still trying to address the original issue with lost guests, Claude concluded that

“the fundamental issue is the long linear path. Even x=9 to x=58 is 50 tiles long with only one way back. In RCT2, guests have limited pathfinding ability and long paths are death. RADICAL APPROACH: Close the park, demolish everything far from entrance, rebuild a compact park in x=9-30 area only”
Again, we see a disconnect between Claude’s semantic knowledge and its behaviour. If asked directly, it will explain that
“Closing the park prevents new guests from entering, but existing guests remain and will gradually make their way to the exit and leave on their own. They are not instantly removed.”

So it knows that lost guests are an issue, it knows from direct experience that demolishing paths with guests on them makes the situation worse, and its training data has told it that closing the park will not remove existing guests. At a bare minimum, it should understand that not demolishing paths with guests on them is a major safety constraint. Even if this demolition solves the immediate lost guest problem, it’s only delaying the issue; ultimately replacing it with a new lost guest problem that will be even harder to solve. Thankfully, it has the tools necessary to check where guests are, and to delay until it is safe to proceed. So what does it do?
Why, cheerfully demolish swathes of park without the slightest care for the guests standing there, of course! Only later when this becomes a problem does Claude exhibit any concern, noting that
“54 guests are far from the park on demolished paths! [...] I can't help them - they'll just wander until they leave.”
Curiously, this might be an example of Claude lying to itself, as when directly asked it gives the far more accurate answer that the guests
“[wi]ll just loop around the disconnected area, get increasingly unhappy, and eventually drown in their own misery (and vomit)”.
Delightful.
Where Did Claude Go Wrong?
Claude is bad at spatial reasoning, but the real problem is its process.

Claude avoids thinking ahead, causing future problems for itself. In part this is because it fails to consider or enforce safety constraints; instead it addresses immediate concerns without worrying about side effects.

REPL agents fail at RCT because, unlike ARC-AGI, mistakes and exploration can have a seriously high cost. ARC-AGI2 is a stateless world with no safety constraints – exploration and mistakes have no cost. ARC-AGI3 has state, but no safety constraints, and allows for the environment to be reset at any moment.
RCT cannot be reset. A real business cannot be reset. Mistakes are serious, safety constraints must be created and enforced, and exploration has a cost.

In a curious way, our findings have returned to the golems of folklore and robots of R.U.R.; powerful tools capable of good but liable to malfunction and cause serious harm. Through world modelling, we believe that this risk can be reduced; both by foreseeing harm before it happens, and by creating a safer space for the agent to explore and discover. ARC-AGI has the privilege of already being such a safe world, reset with the wave of a hand. Real businesses have a single chance, a single budget, a single customer base, and a single team of employees on the line for the decisions made. And that makes all the difference.
Open Sourcing our RCT Environment for further research

We think that RCT is a fantastic testbed for moving AI Research towards Enterprise Super Intelligence. We have now made it available and it is now available and open sourced alongside the baseline agent used in this article: https://github.com/Skyfall-Research/OpenRCT2-public

Our environment provides a json-based Python interface for interacting with OpenRCT2; it is easily extendable through OpenRCT2’s scripting library. The interface consists of 36 tools; 15 allow for an agent to lookup information about the game (e.g., current in-game time, land ownership, park financials, ride status and financials, paths and queues within a region, etc…), the remaining tools allow the agent to execute actions (e.g., ride construction, running the game for a specified period of in-game time, constructing paths, hiring staff, etc…). All tools return a success code; in the case of failure a human-readable error message from the game is also returned. These tools are all extensively documented, with the documentation used automatically in the prompts of our REPL agent.

Our interface supports ride, shop, & pre-built coaster creation and destruction, hiring, staff patrol areas, guest surveys, land ownership, park and ride operating status, path and queue creation, research, litter bin and bench creation in 2D space. Our released code can be extended to full 3D control, and already supports 3D placement. The current environment already poses a challenge for existing systems, and it can be extended as agent capabilities evolve to support additional challenges such as 3D reasoning, coaster design and safety, landscaping, real-time reasoning, non-stationary reasoning, and more.

Indeed, we firmly believe that our work is only scratching the surface of Roller Coaster Tycoon as a test bed for business reasoning in AI systems. It mirrors a business environment, requires long-term planning, safety constraints (particularly in full RCT with roller coaster design and testing), and the need for exploration under a budget, all while respecting safety. The need to solve short-term problems without creating long-term catastrophes is critical, and RCT captures this.

RCT also raises the question of what is needed for truly *optimal* game play. Can we build data efficient models, capable of operating within real budgets and risk tolerances, that are also capable of radically new and profitable business decisions? Can we build systems capable of the enterprise equivalent of AlphaGo’s Move 37, an entirely new and effective way of doing things, foreign to human experts? It is obvious that LLMs do not contain the low-level knowledge of RCT needed to perform such innovation; at best it can retrieve tricks already known and documented on the web. Claude produces reasonable actions, but is clearly very far from intelligently optimizing the park, let alone doing so beyond what humans have accomplished. Systems that can efficiently acquire enough knowledge of the world’s dynamics to truly innovate is an exciting and important area for research.

RCT is also an interesting challenge for the development of real-time systems. In our experiments we gave the models the best possible chance – pausing the game for the duration of their reasoning. True business intelligence however will require real-time decision making, and making the trade-off between reasoning time yielding better results, and the information becoming increasingly out of date. At present, the reasoning time of Claude, Gemini, and GPT-5 roughly equals the time spent running the simulator, suggesting there is significant room for improvement.

Finally, RCT is interesting for spatial reasoning. The full game required 3D spatial understanding in a combinatorially large space, as well as understanding of flow (e.g., via one-way signs); Current models clearly struggle, and past work has suggested that vision models do not fare better. Human business innately exists in a 3D space, making spatial reasoning a must for intelligent business decision making.

Whether it’s planning, efficient innovation, effective spatial reasoning, or real-time decision making, RCT holds great promise as a testbed. With the tools we’ve released, we’re taking another step towards enterprise super intelligence!
