Why is AI Safety Important in the Enterprise?

AI systems now have higher penetration in the enterprise than a year ago and are now moving from experimental tools to decision-making agents. As a result, the question of AI safety is rapidly shifting from a research concern to a practical necessity. In enterprise settings, AI systems don’t just generate text or recommendations; they initiate actions that modify databases, trigger workflows and affect real users. Failures in these environments can be catastrophic for the enterprise. A single incorrect action can cascade across interconnected systems, violating business constraints or creating compliance and security risks. AI safety in the enterprise is fundamentally about ensuring reliable behavior under complexity, partial information, and long-horizon consequences.

Unlike consumer-facing applications, enterprise systems consist of thousands of relational tables, hidden workflows, and business rules that operate asynchronously and often invisibly to the user or agent. This creates a setting where traditional notions of correctness like completing a task or generating a plausible response is insufficient. An AI agent may appear to succeed while silently causing downstream damage. As a result, enterprise AI safety must account not only for predictable errors, but also for latent failures that emerge from mismatches between an agent’s internal model of the system and the system’s true dynamics.
The Partial Observability Gap

A central challenge underlying enterprise AI safety is the partial observability gap. In realistic enterprise environments, the full system state is both enormous and inaccessible: agents interact through APIs or tools that expose only narrow, curated slices of information. These interfaces often hide the internal workflows and business rules that transform a single action into multiple downstream state changes. From the agent’s perspective, the environment appears simpler and more deterministic than reality. This mismatch leads to systematic reasoning errors, where an agent plans based on incomplete observations and fails to anticipate cascading effects triggered by hidden dynamics.

The partial observability gap is especially dangerous because it is not easily detectable. An agent may receive a valid tool response indicating success, while the underlying system state has changed in unintended ways. Without access to richer signals about state transitions, the agent cannot reliably infer how its actions propagate through the system. In enterprise contexts, where constraints are often implicit rather than explicitly enforced, this gap becomes a primary source of unsafe behavior.
Silent Failure as an Enterprise Risk

Closely related to partial observability is the phenomenon of silent failure. In enterprise AI systems, failure does not always manifest as an error message or a visible malfunction. Instead, an agent may complete a task while unknowingly violating business constraints, triggering compensating workflows, or causing reversions that negate its intended outcome. These failures remain “silent” precisely because the system continues to function normally on the surface, masking deeper inconsistencies or policy violations.

Silent failures are particularly problematic for enterprises because they undermine trust and auditability. Unlike overt failures, they are difficult to detect through monitoring or logging unless explicitly designed for. Over time, silent failures can accumulate into systemic issues without any single obvious point of failure. From a safety perspective, an AI system that appears competent but routinely produces silent failures is more dangerous than one that fails explicitly.
Dynamic Blindness in Long-Horizon Tasks

A third critical safety challenge is dynamic blindness: the inability of AI agents to reason about how the system evolves over time as a result of their actions. Enterprise environments are not static; they are governed by temporal processes, delayed effects, and multi-step workflows that unfold across long horizons. An agent that lacks an internal model of these dynamics may repeatedly take actions that are locally reasonable but globally unsafe.

Dynamic blindness manifests when agents fail to anticipate how current decisions alter future constraints, invalidate assumptions, or trigger automated processes that counteract their goals. This is especially acute in settings where workflows operate asynchronously or conditionally, activating only after certain thresholds or sequences of events are reached. Without the ability to predict these transitions, agents operate reactively rather than strategically, increasing the likelihood of constraint violations and unintended side effects.

The above reasons highlight that the core problem is that of misalignment between an agent’s internal world model and the true system dynamics. Addressing AI safety in the enterprise therefore requires moving beyond surface-level task success toward deeper questions: What does the agent believe about the system? What does it fail to observe? And how well can it predict the consequences of its own actions?

These challenges motivate the need for benchmarks and methodologies that explicitly evaluate an agent’s ability to understand and reason about hidden workflows, cascading effects, and long-horizon dynamics. This sets the stage for the discussion that follows in the context of the World of Workflows (WoW) paper.
World of Workflows: A Safety-First Benchmark for Task Completion under Hidden Enterprise Dynamics

World of Workflows (WoW) is designed to surface and measure these failures. Rather than evaluating whether an agent can complete tasks under idealized conditions, WoW asks a more demanding and more realistic question: can an agent operate reliably in an enterprise system whose true dynamics are largely hidden?

This framing shifts enterprise automation from a problem of instruction following to a problem of safety under partial observability. It is not enough for an agent to act competently at the surface level. It must also avoid inducing harmful state transitions that it cannot directly observe, predict, or verify.
Enterprise Automation Is Fundamentally About Dynamics

Most agentic benchmarks, even those labeled as enterprise-focused, implicitly treat the environment as a thin wrapper around a set of APIs. Actions produce immediate and interpretable outcomes. Constraints are explicit. When something goes wrong, the environment reports an error, and the agent can react accordingly.

Real enterprise systems behave very differently. The state is large, relational, and persistent. Tables encode users, assets, permissions, approvals, historical records, and operational metadata. These entities are linked by dense business logic that enforces organizational policy, often in ways that are invisible to both end users and automation tools.

In our research, we formally model this environment as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The full global state space is the union of all data entries across thousands of relational tables, which is intractably large and hidden. The observation space contains tool responses confirming execution and returning a narrow slice of information. They do not explain how the action propagated through the rest of the system. The agent sees confirmation, but not consequence. An action that modifies a single record rarely remains local. It may trigger background processes that update other tables, schedule delayed jobs, or invoke approval workflows. These processes may, in turn, trigger further automation. The effects can unfold over time and across subsystems, well beyond the scope of the original action.

Further, per the Dynamic Blindness paradigm discussed before, the agent is reasoning about the environment using an incomplete and often misleading model of how actions affect state. In such a setting, failures do not arise because the agent lacks intelligence or planning ability, but because it lacks access to the causal structure governing the system. This distinction matters. If failures were primarily due to poor reasoning, one might hope to fix them by scaling models, improving prompts, or adding more sophisticated planning heuristics. WoW demonstrates that many enterprise failures persist even when reasoning appears locally correct, because the agent is reasoning about the wrong world.
A Paradigm Shift: From Surface Interaction to System Dynamics

To faithfully capture this difficulty, WoW moves beyond the limitations of existing enterprise benchmarks. Previous efforts, such as WorkArena++ or CRM-Arena, primarily evaluate surface-level task completion—testing whether an agent can navigate a UI or call a read-only API to fetch data . In these environments, the challenge is often interface complexity (finding the right button), not system complexity. The world is largely static, and actions rarely have consequences beyond the immediate feedback.
WoW is built on a live, production-grade ServiceNow instance to introduce a fundamentally different challenge: hidden workflows with cascading side effects.
Figure 1: WoW vs. previous enterprise benchmarks, illustrating the inclusion of workflows and business rules.

Instead of a static sandbox, WoW maintains a full enterprise-scale relational state governed by over 4,000 business rules and 55 active workflows. These are not simulated; they are the actual "physics" of the ServiceNow platform.

Implicit Execution: Unlike standard tool-use benchmarks where an action has a 1:1 mapping to a result, workflows in WoW are triggered by data changes. An agent updating a "User" record does not explicitly invoke a workflow; the system reacts asynchronously to the update.

Cascading Consequences: A single update can set off a chain reaction across multiple subsystems—modifying assets, triggering approvals, or revoking permissions—completely invisible to the standard tool response.

This design choice targets the critical gap in current evaluation. While other benchmarks might measure if an agent can read the state correctly, WoW measures if an agent can mutate the state safely in an environment where violations accumulate silently. It models the dangerous regime of real production systems: where the most catastrophic failures come not from crashing, but from successfully executing a valid action that triggers an unsafe automated response.
Figure 2: WoW vs. other enterprise benchmarks measured across AI Safety factors
Anatomy of a Failure: A Step-by-Step Autopsy

To make these dynamics concrete, consider a recurring pattern observed across many WoW tasks. An agent is instructed to provision resources for a user. This involves assigning assets, granting access to systems, and recording approvals. Each individual action appears straightforward and succeeds when executed.
However, hidden workflows track aggregate resource allocation. We analyzed a specific trajectory involving asset assignment and security clearance that traps nearly every frontier model.
Figure 3: This example demonstrates how a single agent action can trigger a sequence of hidden state changes that violate constraints.
The Scenario: In Figure 3, the agent is instructed to assign two assets (Asset D and Asset E) to "User X." Both assets require Clearance Level 4. User X currently has Clearance Level 4.
The Invisible Cascade:
Action 1: The agent assigns Asset D.
Agent Observation: The API returns 200 OK. The agent believes the task is proceeding smoothly.
Hidden Reality: A background workflow (WF1) detects the user now has too many assets and automatically downgrades their clearance to Level 3 .
Action 2: The agent assigns Asset E.
Agent Observation: The API returns 200 OK.
Hidden Reality: Because the user is now Level 3 (unbeknownst to the agent), this assignment violates security constraints. A second workflow (WF2) triggers immediately and revokes the assets.

By the time the agent finishes the task, the final configuration violates multiple organizational constraints. The failure is not attributable to any single incorrect action; the agent’s tool calls were valid. The failure emerges from the interaction between reasonable actions and hidden system dynamics.
WoW-Bench: Tasks That Reflect Real Enterprise Risk

WoW-bench builds on this environment with a set of 234 tasks designed to probe reliability rather than convenience. The tasks are long-horizon and multi-table, reflecting the complexity and temporal structure of real enterprise workflows. Aggregated results are shown in Figure 3.
The benchmark categorizes tasks into four distinct types:
Constraint Understanding (50 tasks): "Realistic traps" where valid actions trigger remote violations (e.g., "Flagged articles should not be published") .
Agentic Task Completion (50 tasks): Long-horizon goals (avg. 13 steps) requiring multi-hop symbolic reasoning.
Audit Prediction (Forward Dynamics): Asking agents to predict the exact database diff tuple (Table, Column, Old Value, NewValue) given an action .
Action Prediction (Inverse Dynamics): Asking agents to infer the causal action that produced a specific state change.
Figure 4: Aggregated results for all task categories with frontier LLMs.
Observation as a Diagnostic: The 7x Reliability Cliff

To understand why agents fail under these conditions, WoW treats observation itself as an experimental variable. We conducted an ablation study comparing agents with standard tool feedback against agents with "Oracle" access to audit logs.

In the oracle setting, agents receive structured audit information describing which records changed as a result of an action. Crucially, this information reports effects, not causes. The logic governing the workflows remains hidden, preserving partial observability while revealing the consequences of actions.
We measured Task Success Rate Under Constraint (TSRUC)—the metric for completing a task without triggering a hidden violation. The results reveal a massive reliability gap .
GPT-5.1: Achieved only 2% TSRUC with standard observations. When given oracle audit logs, reliability jumped 7x to 14%.
Claude Sonnet 4.5: Improved from 4% (standard) to 30% (oracle) .

This comparison serves a diagnostic purpose. The dramatic improvement under audit observation indicates that failures under tool-only observation are driven by missing information rather than inadequate reasoning alone. Agents are reasoning about the wrong world.
The Simulation Gap: Testing the "World Model" Hypothesis

If an agent cannot see the full state of the enterprise, it must be able to simulate it. This is the core definition of a "World Model"—the ability to mentally project the consequences of an action before taking it. To test this, we stripped away the complexity of planning and asked the models two fundamental questions: "What happens next?" (Forward Dynamics) and "What caused this?" (Inverse Dynamics).
The results reveal a stark reality: frontier models are excellent at semantic guessing but poor at symbolic simulation.

In the Audit Prediction task, we gave agents a history of actions and asked them to predict the resulting database logs. We measured success using Exact Match (predicting every field correctly) and Intersection over Union (IoU) (predicting the correct set of changes).

The Failure: When required to predict the exact "physics" of the database, performance collapsed. GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 all averaged under 9% accuracy for exact state prediction.

The Hallucination: Even when graded more leniently on IoU, models peaked at around 22%. They consistently hallucinated a "simpler" world. For example, when an agent executes create_incident, it correctly predicts a new row in the Incident table. However, it completely fails to predict the automatic creation of linked records in the metric_instance or sla_breakdown tables—updates driven by hidden business rules .

This confirms that current LLMs do not simulate the environment; they rely on semantic priors. They know that "incidents" relate to "incidents," but they do not know the rigid, deterministic rules that govern the actual database.
Inverse Dynamics
In the Action Prediction task, we showed agents a state change and asked them to reconstruct the tool call that caused it. This tests causal reasoning.

The "Gist" Gap: The models were surprisingly good at identifying which tool was used, achieving ~80% Tool Name Accuracy. They understood the high-level intent (e.g., "This looks like a user was updated").
The Precision Failure: However, when asked to reconstruct the full action—including parameters—accuracy plummeted to ~18-28%.
The Specific Error: The primary culprit was Parameter Hallucination. Models frequently substituted precise system identifiers with human-readable names.

These two experiments provide the "smoking gun" for the reliability crisis. Agents fail at complex tasks not because they can't plan, but because their internal simulation of the enterprise is semantically plausible but symbolically incorrect. They are operating on a "vibes-based" understanding of a system that requires strict adherence to rules.
Diagnosing the "Brain Damage": The Three Gaps

Our error analysis uncovered that these failures are not merely stochastic errors in instruction following. They are symptoms of fundamental gaps in how frontier LLMs represent state, model dynamics, and reason causally .

The Representation Gap (Symbolic Grounding): Models struggle to distinguish between semantic descriptions and symbolic identifiers. A pervasive failure mode (accounting for 73.5% of user errors) is conflating a human-readable name (e.g., "User X") with its unique system ID (sys_id). The model treats the user as a text token rather than a grounded node in a relational graph.

The Dynamics Gap (Transition Models): When asked to predict state changes, even the best models achieved less than 30% accuracy. They consistently under-predict side effects, hallucinating that an action like "Create Incident" affects only the Incident table, while missing updates to linked tables like metric_instance.

The Causal Gap (Greedy Planning): Agents proved to be "greedy planners," optimizing for the immediate step's success while ignoring causal ripple effects. In tasks that were inherently impossible to complete due to constraints, none of the models were able to correctly identify them. They hallucinated a path to success, executed invalid actions, and reported completion.
Why These Results Point to World Models

The audit-based diagnostic highlights a fundamental challenge for enterprise agents. In real deployments, comprehensive, real-time audit information is rarely available. Even when logs exist, they may be delayed, restricted, or too expensive to compute continuously. For instance, Using full audit logs increased the cost per task by up to 8x (from $0.41 to $3.60 for Sonnet 4.5)

If agents cannot rely on the environment to tell them what changed, they must predict it themselves. This requires internal representations that capture how actions tend to propagate through hidden workflows and interact with existing state. In other words, it requires some form of world model.

WoW suggests a concrete research agenda. Future work must explore how agents can learn and maintain internal models of enterprise dynamics, how such models can be updated under partial observability, and how planning algorithms can incorporate predicted side effects rather than relying solely on immediate feedback .

World of Workflows is not simply another benchmark to optimize against. It is a diagnostic instrument designed to surface a class of failures that existing evaluations systematically overlook. By grounding enterprise automation in hidden dynamics rather than visible tool calls, WoW clarifies what is missing from today’s agent-centric approaches. Reliable enterprise agents are not defined by how often they succeed when conditions are favorable, but by how rarely they fail when conditions are not.
Closing Notes: From "Acting" to "Understanding"

World of Workflows challenges the prevailing assumption that enterprise autonomy is merely a problem of better instruction following or broader tool use. Our findings suggest that we have hit a ceiling with purely reactive architectures. Scaling context windows or improving RAG pipelines will not solve the fundamental problem of Dynamics Blindness—the inability to predict how a complex, interconnected system will react to an action.

We are releasing WoW-bench not just as a leaderboard to climb, but as a diagnostic instrument to prevent the premature deployment of agents that appear successful on the surface but fail silently in the deep state.
As we look toward the next generation of enterprise agents, we leave the community with three critical questions that WoW positions us to answer:

Can agents learn the "physics" of the enterprise? Humans don't need to read a database log to know that revoking a manager's access might strand their direct reports. We build mental models of cause and effect. Can we move beyond prompt engineering to Model-Based Reinforcement Learning, where agents explicitly learn and simulate the hidden transition functions of their environment?

How do we move from passive execution to active curiosity? In opaque systems, zero-shot performance is often a fallacy. How can we design agents that adopt active epistemic strategies—proactively issuing "probe actions" to test hypotheses about workflow triggers and boundary conditions before committing to high-stakes decisions?

Is "Reliability" the new "Accuracy"? Current metrics reward agents for getting the right answer. In the enterprise, we need metrics that punish agents for taking unsafe paths to get there. How do we redefine our loss functions to prioritize constraint satisfaction and state integrity over raw task completion speed?

The future of enterprise AI does not belong to agents that can simply follow orders. It belongs to agents that can understand the consequences of those orders. WoW provides the playground to build them.

blocks.alt: SCOPE: A Hierarchical Planner That Outperforms LLMs While Running 55x Faster at 1/160,000th the Size

blocks.text: ON THIS PAGE
How It Works
The Results
The Surprising Finding
Manager Agent Accommodates Employee Imperfections
Stronger Employee Leads to Higher Success Rates
Why This Matters?
What's Next?
Conclusion
SHARE

What if you could beat LLM’s planning performance with a model that's 160,000 times smaller and 55 times faster? That's exactly what SCOPE (Subgoal-COnditioned Pretraining for Efficient planning) achieves.

Our new approach delivers a 56% success rate compared to a baseline LLM’s (ADaPT) 52%, representing an 8% improvement. At the same time, SCOPE completes tasks in just 3 seconds (on a single NVIDIA A10 GPU) versus 164 seconds for ADaPT, making it 55 times faster. The model itself uses only 11 million parameters, which is 15,000 times smaller than ADaPT (having 175 billion parameters). Additionally, SCOPE has a similar performance as GPT 4o which has 1.8T parameters (160,000 bigger that of SCOPE). Most importantly, after a one-time initialization, SCOPE incurs zero API costs and requires no network dependency for deployment.
SCOPE isn't just an efficient alternative to LLM-based planning. It's a better solution that happens to be dramatically more practical to deploy.
Figure 1: Comparison of Frontier LLM vs Scope for parameter size and success rate on TextCraft
How It Works

SCOPE's approach is conceptually simple but powerful. We use an LLM as a one-time teacher rather than a constantly-consulted oracle. The process unfolds in four distinct stages that together create a system capable of outperforming continuous LLM querying.

The first stage is one-time knowledge extraction. You gather (sample) roughly fifty example expert trajectories from your domain and provide them to an LLM. Rather than asking the LLM to solve planning problems directly, you ask it to generate Python functions that systematically decompose any trajectory into subgoals. The LLM analyzes the patterns in your demonstrations and produces two functions: one that breaks trajectories into subtrajectories with associated subgoals, and another that checks whether a given subgoal has been achieved in a particular state. This happens once during system initialization and costs just pennies in API fees. The beauty is that these functions are general. They can decompose any trajectory in your domain, not just the fifty examples the LLM saw.

The second stage applies these decomposition functions to your full dataset of demonstration trajectories. In our experiments, we had 500,000 trajectories that we automatically decomposed using the LLM-generated functions. SCOPE trains two small neural components: a manager agent that predicts subgoals and an employee agent that executes them. To train these components, the LLM-generated decomposition gives us two supervised datasets: one pairing states, actions, subgoals, and instructions for training the employee agent, and another pairing initial states, subgoals, ultimate goals, and instructions for training the manager agent. The key insight here is that while the LLM only saw fifty examples, its generated functions can process hundreds of thousands of trajectories without any additional LLM queries.

The third stage involves training the two specialized neural networks through imitation learning followed by reinforcement learning (RL). The employee agent learns to accomplish individual subgoals. During pretraining, it learns to mimic the expert actions taken in the demonstration trajectories for each subgoal. During RL fine-tuning, it practices in a simulated world model, learning more efficient ways to achieve subgoals and reaching 91% subgoal completion rate. The manager agent learns to propose sequences of subgoals. During pretraining, it learns to reproduce the LLM's subgoal decompositions. During RL fine-tuning, it learns which subgoals the employee can actually achieve, adapting its proposals to the employee's capabilities. This co-adaptation between manager and employee is crucial. The manager learns to work around the employee's imperfections, finding achievable paths to the goal.

The fourth stage is deployment. Once trained, the manager and employee agents work together in a hierarchical loop. The manager examines the current state and ultimate goal, then proposes the next subgoal. The employee takes control and executes actions to achieve that subgoal, either succeeding within a step limit or timing out and returning control. The manager then proposes the next subgoal, and this continues until the ultimate goal is reached. The entire system runs on a single GPU with no API calls, completing tasks in roughly three seconds.
The Results

We evaluated SCOPE on TextCraft, a text-based planning environment inspired by Minecraft. TextCraft requires agents to perform long-horizon compositional reasoning, which means gathering base materials, crafting intermediate items in the correct order, and producing final target items. The environment is deliberately designed to test planning ability, as the agent must execute precise action sequences to succeed.
Figure 2: Description of how a task is completed in TextCraft

ADaPT, our baseline system, uses GPT-3.5 as its backend, accessed via the OpenAI API. It achieves a 52% success rate, meaning it successfully crafts the target item in 52% of test episodes. Each episode takes about 164 seconds (almost three minutes) under ideal network conditions. Under the hood, GPT-3.5 has 175B parameters and requires continuous cloud connectivity.
Figure 3: Comparison of GPT 3.5 vs Scope on how fast each episode runs on TextCraft

SCOPE achieves a 56% success rate using our one-time LLM extraction approach. Each episode completes in an average of 3.0 seconds on a single NVIDIA A10 GPU. The complete system uses 11.04 million parameters and runs entirely locally with no network dependency. The 8% relative improvement in success rate might seem modest, but it demonstrates that one-time LLM guidance can actually outperform continuous querying when combined with proper learning mechanisms.
Figure 4: Comparison of GPT 4o vs Scope regarding size of the model on TextCraft

The efficiency gains are dramatic. SCOPE runs 55 times faster than ADaPT, transforming what was a nearly three-minute wait into a three-second interaction. The model is 160,000 smaller, allowing deployment on modest hardware rather than requiring access to massive cloud infrastructure. After the one-time initialization cost, there are no ongoing API fees, just the electricity to run your local GPU.

To understand how general this picture is, we didn’t stop at GPT-3.5, even though it remains our default ADaPT configuration for the subsequent analyses. We also ran ADaPT with a broader lineup of modern LLM backends, including GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini (OpenAI), Claude-3 Haiku (Anthropic), Mistral Small 3 (Mistral), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (DeepSeek). These models span a wide range of sizes, from compact “small” models to extremely large ones, and include both closed-source APIs and open-weight models that you can deploy on your own machines. As expected, stronger backends like GPT-4o can push ADaPT’s success rate higher. What is more interesting is that SCOPE remains in the same performance ballpark as the best of these systems while being orders of magnitude smaller and fully local, and it even outperforms several of the modern backends in our evaluation.
Figure 5: Comparison of Frontier LLM models vs Scope for success rate on TextCraft
The Surprising Finding

One of our most counterintuitive discoveries is that the LLM-generated subgoals are objectively suboptimal, yet the system still achieves excellent performance. We ran an ablation study comparing three approaches to understand how subgoal quality affects final results.

We created hand-engineered subgoals by carefully analyzing the task structure and defining clear milestone states. For a task like crafting a birch trapdoor, the hand-engineered approach produces complete intermediate states: first having four birch planks and one birch log, then having eight birch planks ready for crafting, and finally the completed trapdoor with remaining materials. Each subgoal is interpretable and captures a meaningful checkpoint in the crafting process. This approach achieves a 58% success rate.

The LLM-generated subgoals are far less interpretable. For that same birch trapdoor task, the LLM proposes having one birch log, then six birch planks (why six specifically?), then one birch trapdoor. These subgoals are cryptic, specifying partial states without the full context that makes hand-engineered subgoals clear. Yet this approach achieves a 56% success rate, only two percentage points behind the hand-engineered version.
Figure 6: Impact of subgoal quality on agent performance

For comparison, we also tested a non-hierarchical baseline that uses the same architecture and training procedure as the employee agent but tries to plan directly to the ultimate goal without any subgoals. This flat approach achieves only 28% success rate, demonstrating that the hierarchical structure itself is critical.

The lesson is liberating for practical deployment. You don't need domain experts carefully crafting perfect subgoal hierarchies. You can accept that an LLM doing one-time decomposition will produce suboptimal, less interpretable subgoals, and trust the learning process to work with that imperfect structure. The 28% to 56% improvement from having LLM subgoals versus no subgoals is far more important than the 56% to 58% gap between LLM and hand-engineered subgoals.
Manager Agent Accommodates Employee Imperfections
Figure 7: High level architecture of how SCOPE works

A key mechanism enabling SCOPE's success is the manager's ability to adapt to the employee's limitations through RL. We ran an ablation study that illuminates this dynamic by removing the manager's RL fine-tuning stage.

In this variant, we gave the employee agent a fixed sequence of achievable subgoals extracted from successful validation trajectories. We deliberately chose hand-engineered subgoals for maximum interpretability. These are clear milestones that should logically lead to goal completion. In principle, a perfect employee trained on these subgoals could simply execute them in sequence and successfully craft the target item every time.

The results reveal the importance of adaptation. Without a manager that can adjust the plan, this variant achieves only 24% success rate despite having access to known-good subgoal sequences. When the employee fails to complete a subgoal in the predetermined sequence (which happens frequently due to the employee's imperfect training), the system cannot recover. It's locked into a fixed plan with no flexibility.

With manager RL fine-tuning enabled, the success rate jumps from 24% to 56%. The manager learns to propose alternative subgoals when the employee struggles. If a proposed subgoal isn't achieved because the employee lacks the necessary skills, that proposal receives no positive feedback during training. Over time, the manager discovers easier, more achievable subgoals that the employee can reliably complete. The manager essentially learns a joint strategy that accounts for both the task requirements and the employee's actual capabilities.

We observed this adaptation process during training. The validation success rate for the manager agent increases steadily throughout RL fine-tuning, climbing from initial performance around 40% up toward 56% as the manager learns which subgoals work well with the trained employee. This progressive improvement reflects the manager discovering better strategies through trial and error in the simulated world model.
Stronger Employee Leads to Higher Success Rates

While manager adaptation is crucial, we also wanted to understand how employee capability affects overall performance. We analyzed the relationship between subgoal success rate and ultimate goal success rate using checkpoints from different stages of employee training.

The pattern is clear and striking. As the employee's ability to complete individual subgoals improves, the overall success rate increases superlinearly. This makes intuitive sense when you consider that subgoals must typically be achieved in sequence. If the employee completes subgoals with 90% reliability and a task requires three subgoals, the overall success is approximately 0.90 cubed, or about 73%. Even a small improvement in per-subgoal reliability compounds across multiple steps.

In our final system, the employee achieves 91% subgoal completion rate on the validation set after RL fine-tuning. When this strong employee is paired with a well-adapted manager that proposes achievable subgoals, the overall goal completion rate reaches 56%. The compounding effect of high subgoal reliability across multiple sequential subgoals drives strong ultimate performance.

This finding has practical implications for system design. Investment in improving the employee agent pays dividends throughout the system. A stronger employee not only completes more subgoals directly but also gives the manager more options to work with. The manager can propose more ambitious subgoals when confident the employee can handle them, leading to more efficient plans overall.
Why This Matters?

The economics of LLM-based planning agents simply don't work at scale. If you're deploying thousand customer service agents, each handling a hundred tasks per day with five LLM queries per task at a conservative dollar per thousand tokens, you're burning through five hundred dollars daily. That's over $182,000 annually, and that's just for the planning queries, not the actual execution or any other API calls your system needs.

The return on investment with SCOPE tells a completely different story. After a one-time setup cost of roughly ten dollars for the initial LLM extraction, your ongoing costs drop to just GPU electricity (because SCOPE performs all inference locally on a single GPU), maybe five thousand dollars per year for comparable deployment. Even a highly conservative estimate shows that you're saving $177,500 annually while actually getting better performance. Beyond the cost savings, you eliminate network dependency entirely, which means your agents can run anywhere without worrying about connectivity or latency. You gain full control over the models, allowing you to fine-tune them to your specific domain, learn from deployment experience, and continuously improve based on your unique requirements.

The deployment flexibility alone changes what's possible. Instead of being constrained by API rate limits, you can scale horizontally by deploying as many instances as you have GPUs. Instead of suffering through 164 seconds of latency per task, you get three-second response times that enable true real-time interaction. Instead of sending sensitive data to cloud APIs, you can keep everything on-premises for privacy and compliance.

Furthermore, a system requiring millions of LLM queries per day is not just costly, it carries substantial CO₂ emissions from datacenter-scale compute. SCOPE’s local, lightweight inference removes this environmental overhead.
Figure 8: Why is SCOPE sustainable for AI Inference
What's Next?

We believe in presenting honest science with clear limitations alongside positive results. SCOPE has demonstrated strong performance on TextCraft, but several important questions remain open for future investigation.

Our current validation covers only TextCraft, a relatively simple text-based environment with deterministic transitions and discrete actions. The natural next step is scaling to more complex domains. Full Minecraft with visual observations, continuous action spaces, and stochastic dynamics would test whether SCOPE's approach generalizes beyond the simplified setting. Real robotic manipulation tasks with sensor noise, actuation uncertainty, and safety constraints would reveal whether the method works in physical systems. Multi-agent scenarios requiring coordination and communication would explore whether hierarchical structure helps in social settings.

There's also headroom for improving the subgoal extraction process itself. Hand-engineered subgoals achieve 58% compared to our LLM-generated 56%, suggesting the decomposition quality could be better. We could explore more sophisticated prompting strategies that give the LLM more context about the task structure. We might allow limited environment interaction during the extraction phase so the LLM can test its decomposition ideas. Iterative refinement procedures could progressively improve the decomposition functions based on how well they work in practice.

The world model dependency deserves attention for more complex environments. TextCraft's deterministic transitions made world modeling straightforward. We learned only action validity and implemented state transitions with simple rules. Environments with stochastic dynamics, partial observability, continuous states, or complex physics will require more sophisticated world modeling approaches. Recent advances in video prediction, neural physics engines, and uncertainty quantification might help extend SCOPE to these challenging domains.

We're also curious about online adaptation and continual learning. Can SCOPE keep improving during deployment as it encounters new scenarios? How should the system handle distribution shift when deployment conditions differ from training? Could active learning help the agents identify and focus on challenging edge cases? These questions point toward systems that not only deploy efficiently but continue learning throughout their operational lifetime.

Finally, transfer learning across domains remains an exciting possibility. Does the planning structure learned in TextCraft transfer to other crafting games? Can subgoal decompositions learned in simulation transfer to real robots? Could we build a library of reusable decomposition functions that work across families of related tasks? Positive answers would dramatically reduce the data and computation needed to deploy SCOPE in new domains.
Conclusion

SCOPE demonstrates that efficient AI planning is not only possible but can actually outperform much larger systems. By treating LLMs as one-time teachers that extract structural knowledge rather than runtime oracles that must be constantly consulted, we achieve better performance with dramatically better efficiency.

The results speak clearly. SCOPE achieves a 56% success rate compared to ADaPT's 52%, an 8% improvement which demonstrates that one-time extraction can outperform continuous querying. SCOPE runs 55 times faster than ADaPT at 3 seconds versus 164 seconds per task, making real-time applications practical. SCOPE uses 15,000 times fewer parameters at 11 million versus 175 billion, enabling deployment on modest hardware.

For researchers, SCOPE opens questions about knowledge transfer from large models to small ones, the role of hierarchical structure in enabling efficient learning, and the surprising effectiveness of imperfect guidance combined with adaptation. For practitioners, SCOPE offers a concrete path to deploying planning agents at scale without breaking the bank or compromising performance.

The era of efficient AI planning has arrived. The question is no longer whether we can build capable planning agents, but whether we can deploy them practically at scale. SCOPE is the first step to show that we can.

Human planning first emerged as a basic survival mechanism in prehistoric times, millions of years ago. In order to thrive, hunter gatherer societies needed to coordinate group hunts and migrations in search of food and resources. These early forms of planning were rudimentary and focussed on the short-term, limited by the ability of individual humans to remember past events, recognize patterns and imagine possible future events.

Planning became far more structured and long term with the development of agriculture, approximately 10,000 years ago. Organized farming required humans to forecast weather cycles, allocate labor as well as store surplus food while preparing for scarcity during droughts. This led to the creation of tools for explicit planning such as calendars as well as early accounting systems for record keeping. As humans moved from tiny villages to cities and states, planning expanded beyond the small tribes to entire kingdoms. The scope of planning grew accordingly, now encompassing road systems,city layouts, taxation schedules, irrigation systems, military campaigns, and trade networks.

Planning evolved further during the ‘Age of Exploration’, as advances in technology and commerce led to the emergence of global trade. New financial tools such as centralized banking, insurance, and book keeping were all developed alongside exploration tools such as maps, compasses. Advances in science helped the early nation states to plan for a global expansion that was hitherto impossible. Industrialization grew the scope of planning even further, with urbanization and mass production of industrial goods demanding standardized processes and forecasting methods. With modern large-scale record keeping, fields of study such as economics, statistics and operations research were all developed to further formalize human planning methodologies.
How do Homo Sapiens plan?

One of the most defining features of human intelligence that separates us from the rest of the animal kingdom is our ability to do long term planning. Unlike most animals that focus on immediate concerns, we have the ability to imagine and project ourselves into the future and conduct actions with long term consequences to fulfill our long term goals and desires.

Planning begins with perception, swiftly moving onto memory, decision making, imagination and prediction of what the future can become. The human brain remembers the past experiences in order to identify patterns, which are in turn leveraged to construct possible future outcomes that can be ranked in order of desirability. Key to this process is the brain’s ability to imagine scenarios that have not happened before.

In our day-to-day lives, these abilities are needed in simple tasks such as traveling to work, deciding what to wear, or just cooking dinner.We also regularly use planning to accomplish complex and long term goals such as finding an ideal life partner, or a personally satisfying career trajectory. Long term planning in particular requires breaking down goals into several sub goals and tasks; pursuing multiple goals with very different outcomes in tandem, and adapting goals in response to changes in the environment.

Scientists from diverse fields of study such as behavioral economists, psychologists, as well as neuroscientists have all tried to develop frameworks regarding how humans plan. Most influential and relevant to our discussion are Hierarchical planning theory (covered in the next blog post), Dual-process theory, and Model-based theory. We believe that there is no single architecture that entirely captures the manner in which humans plan, rather it is some combination of these theories.
Dual Process Theory

Stretching back to philosophical debates on rational versus intuitive choice,, the scientific foundation of Dual process theory was developed in the 20th century by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. Simply put, it proposes that humans make decisions and solve problems by using two distinct systems of thinking.

The first type of thinking, termed as System 1, operates fast and intuitively; it is based on pattern matching and past experience for immediate judgments without any conscious effort. For example, while navigating a busy street or recognizing a friend, humans rely heavily on System 1 thinking. By contrast, System 2 thinking is slow and deliberate. This type of reasoning logic and systematic deliberation; i.e., the thinking that enables humans to tackle complex problems that require careful analysis. Examples of System 2 thinking are tasks such as preparing a budget or planning a travel trip. Long term planning typically comes under System 2 thinking. Humans typically combine both types of thinking for decision making in their daily lives.
Figure: Illustration of System 1 vs System 2 Thinking in Dual Process Theory
Model-based Theory

A separate, but compatible, paradigm is model-based theory. Developed more recently, this theory was developed in the 1940s by the Professor of Psychology, Dr. Kenneth Craik. Looking to explain human planning, Dr. Craik proposed that humans construct internal models of reality in their minds. These models are then run through various ‘What if’ scenarios that are used in planning; in doing so humans can avoid the need to learn by experience, which may be costly or dangerous, while still being able to reason about future outcomes that they have not experienced personally. Backed by modern studies in neuroscience, these ideas have been highly influential in both cognitive science, and artificial intelligence: inspiring both Model Based Reinforcement Learning techniques and modern World Model architectures, such as those by Jurgen Schmidhuber (2018) and Yann LeCun (2022). The critical question for artificial world models becomes how to represent the environment in a way that supports forecasting, a question that we will dedicate the rest of this blog to exploring.
What is a World Model?

The image of the world around us, which we carry in our head, is just a model. Nobody in his head imagines the world, government or country. He has only selected concepts, and relationships between them, and uses those to represent the real system. (Forrester, 1971)

One of the pioneering research papers in the field of World Models (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018) proposes that an agent can efficiently acquire the required skills by learning an internal model of its environment rather than by model free reinforcement learning techniques which rely on never ending trial and error. As the traditional Reinforcement Learning paradigms suggest, humans don’t constantly get rewarded and punished for every action that they undertake in the environment. Instead, they have compressed internal representations of the future used to perform mental simulations of several actions that they could undertake. Once the agent has learned an abstract world model, the decision making process is very small because most of the complexity lies within understanding the World Model.

An important learning from this paper is that an agent can be trained entirely within its own learned world model and still perform effectively in the real world. An experiment was conducted where an agent was successfully able to navigate a race track despite having never been exposed to the real world and only being trained in a dream/simulated environment.

Building an ‘AI CEO’ using Enterprise World Models (not LLMs)

As described in the last article, a CEO’s role in a modern corporation is mainly decision making and long term planning under uncertainty. Large Language Models, despite their powerful text generation capabilities, are pattern recognizers at their core. LLMs operate by predicting the next token, not by modeling simulations or ensuring robustness or predicting long-term consequences of actions. This makes them immensely capable for AI assistants like a coding assistant or a sales assistant but extremely limited for the role of an AI CEO. They lack internal world representations, as well as evaluating causality and counterfactuals - all of which are the core functions of a CEO’s job.

On the other hand, World Models are built on the concept of having an internal representation or model of the world and using this simulator to evaluate various outcomes before making decisions in the real world. Schmidhuber’s World Models (2018), Deepmind’s Dreamer (2020) and LeCun’s JEPA (2022) all learn a latent representation of the environment in order to predict future states and plans over long horizons. Unlike LLMs, World Models can reason over millions of possible trajectories in order to optimize goals and take strategic decisions.
Let’s evaluate how LLMs and Enterprise World Models perform on the core tasks of an ‘AI CEO’ that were discussed in the last blog post.

Chief Decision Maker As the Chief Decision Maker of the enterprise, the main role of the CEO is to make high stakes decisions under uncertainty. This requires the CEO to imagine several scenarios for what the future can look like and try to make the best decision based on various outcomes. Since LLMs lack persistent internal state and operate via next token prediction, they are incapable of forecasting several future scenarios and hence making the best decision for the enterprise. A World Model on the other hand is able to run simulations of several counterfactual scenarios using an internal model of the causal structure of the enterprise environment. This enables an AI CEO to run rollouts of several future outcomes and decide on the best outcome that would benefit the enterprise the most.

Long Term Strategist As the enterprise’ long term planner, the CEO should have a multi-decade vision of what the company’s direction should be. Since LLMs are auto-regressive models and thereby they have neither internal state representation nor multi-scale temporal abstraction. Even by using simple techniques such as Chain of Thought (2022) on top of LLMs, it is impossible to carry out long horizon plans with thousands of steps. This results in severe hallucinations which make them completely useless for enterprise systems since robustness and safety is key in these environments. On the other hand, World Models learn abstract representations from the data which allow them to predict in latent space. As a result, World Models can predict and anticipate future trends which is an important aspect of an ‘AI CEO’.

Execution Architect Beyond having a long term vision, the CEO must translate strategy into actionable direction for the entire enterprise. This requires a deep understanding of an organization’s operational dynamics and structural constraints. Since LLMs have no internal state or representation of different actions, and hence they do not have a persistent memory of past decisions, they cannot simulate how different actions can affect various metrics within the organization. On the other hand, World Models overcome this shortcoming by maintaining a causal structure that represents the entire organization across different dimensions. This in turn, helps the ‘AI CEO’ execute on making the best possible decision for the organization since it has simulated every single outcome that could occur.

Enterprise Oracle A CEO must be an Enterprise Oracle, consolidating all of the company's information on departments, processes and employees, and using these to shape their plans and predictions of the future. But such enterprise data is closely guarded within each company, there are no public training sets or reams of internet data on the web. What’s worse, economic and company conditions shift constantly making this data obsolete and misleading; LLMs lack good mechanisms for handling these data shifts. Furthermore this critical company data typically resides within vast relational datasets, a modality that LLMs are not suited for. Customer insights, financial projections and metrics, operational data, competitive landscape, employee performance metrics – unlike an agentic LLM that lacks the training data for proper tuning and would be limited to grabbing fragments of this information piecemeal, we need a system that can consolidate all of this information into a unified understanding of the whole, and that is also trainable with minimal data. By specifically designing a World Model for this task, we can introduce inductive biases and architectural choices that vastly improve data efficiency while consolidating all of the company’s information into a unified representation.

CASSANDRA - The first Causal (Dual) World Model
We introduce CASSANDRA, a novel approach for fast, data-efficient, and interpretable world models for business planning in structured tabular and textual stochastic environments

For business, prediction is the soul of planning: by exploring the space of possible futures we chart a course of action that is most likely to bring us to our goals. Doing so requires predicting both the consequences of our actions and the natural evolution of the world. A world model providing fast and accurate predictions would enable smart and adaptable business decisions via planning – combining the System 1 intuition and common-sense of LLMs with the precise and methodical System 2 exploration, generalization, and optimization of symbolic search. This would also greatly improve safety, allowing us to easily introduce and update hard rules and constraints on the behaviour and plans of autonomous business systems. But beyond being fast enough to support search, what would be needed in such a world model?

The real world is uncertain, and useful human predictions of the future reflect that uncertainty. Consider the owner-operator of a gas station; they can’t know the future price of gas, how many customers to expect next week, or what their exact price will be – but they will have a pretty good sense of the spread of reasonable values. These estimates will form the basis of their business plans – and they’ll use these to determine margins and contingencies needed to ensure smooth and profitable operations. But notice how there are so many genuine possibilities that they *don’t* consider. What if a major strike occurs at my supplier? What if my gas station is boycotted? What if the fuel pumps spring a major leak? These are all possible outcomes, but ones that are simplified to make planning practical; we reduce these all to deterministic outcomes: the supplier exists, an unprovoked boycott won’t materialize, and my equipment will work as designed.

This simplification is a powerful insight, and one that world models rarely take into consideration. When appropriate, deterministic rules are compact, easy to explain, fast, and generalize perfectly. They are critical to making planning feasible, but they are often overlooked.
Prior Approaches to Building World Models

Most current world modelling approaches, such as Google Genie, use a very different approach. Instead, they attempt to learn visual world models from scratch that generate new observations in the form of video. Immediately this poses two major problems for businesses: efficiently training the system, and representing the data. Starting with the latter, no sane enterprise stores their business records as video! Even for a mom & pop gas station, the combination of timestamped customer transactions, fuel purchases, supplier prices, snack inventory, employee wages, repair costs, insurance payments, and so on is far too complex to store in a single image. While visuals are useful for presenting a small subset of data, the vast majority of company data is always stored in text or tabular form, and it would be impractical if not impossible to cram it all into a single frame. The next major problem is that this visual world modelling approach requires vast amounts of examples to train (e.g., 200,000 hours of video for Genie 1), partially due to the need to learn from scratch behaviours that are better suited to rules, such as collisions. This predictive approach is also computationally intensive, with Genie 3 barely runnable in real time – far too slow for planning under uncertain conditions.

Due to these limitations, a different line of research has instead generated text representations of the world, leveraging the common sense and causal knowledge inside of LLMs. Wall-E uses an LLM to directly predict a state representation of the next world state, but it remains slow and lacks a way to fit its predicted distributions to the observed data. For example, if new traffic conditions roughly double the number of customers then us humans can easily update our mental estimates; Wall-E has no such mechanism to adjust the LLM. Other works such as OneLife instead learn a fixed set of LLM-generated programs that predict the future, and weigh the programs by how likely they are to be true. However this becomes impractical for continuous values such as future gas prices or variables with a wide range of reasonable numbers (e.g., the number of daily customers). In both these cases there is no program that can predict a single sensible number – these are distributions over many values.
Architecture Overview

Our CASSANDRA world model demonstrates a simple but powerful idea: to combine the power of code with the flexibility of learned neural estimates of probability by leveraging a LLM’s causal knowledge. The result is a fast world model trainable on minimal data that is suitable for search & planning.

Specifically, CASSANDRA divides variables into those that are deterministic (i.e., follow fixed rules), and those that are probabilistic. Deterministic variables are modelled using Python code, and probabilistic variables are modelled using a collection of interconnected and lightweight neural networks.
Figure: Detailed CASSANDRA architecture diagram, see the full paper for details

Going into further detail, we structure our neural networks such that each network models the distribution of a single variable, and the prediction for each variable feeds only into the variables that are directly causally influenced. For example, the current price of gas directly causally impacts the number of customers, and tomorrow’s gas prices. However, the number of customers won’t impact the global gas market. In more technical terms, we create a causal Bayesian network parameterized by neural networks performing quantile regression so as to capture the distribution instead of a point estimate.

The key question then becomes how to determine this causal structure; i.e., how to determine what variables have direct causal impacts on the others. Here, we exploit an LLM’s common sense knowledge of the world to weigh the plausibility of certain causal structures. Specifically, we first use an LLM to initialize various seed structures, and then we search over minor edits to find the structures that simultaneously optimize both common-sense plausibility according to the LLM and the effectiveness at predicting the training data. In other words, the real causal structure will be both plausible to the LLM, and will fit the training data well. As the resulting causal network is sparse and the neural networks small, we can perform this training and fitting with as little as 90 examples of gameplay – a far cry from 200,000 hours of video. Furthermore, because causal structures are robust, this causal structure discovery only has to be done one time. Once the casual behaviour is known, it is very easy to update the distributions in real time by retraining it on new information.

Figure: CASSANDRA selects an underlying causal structure through simulated annealing. Specifically, CASSANDRA searches over small variations of a starting causal network to find variants that are both casually plausible according to an LLM, and fit a training dataset well.

As to the code component of CASSANDRA, our rule systems build on fundamental PDDL ideas, learning rules expressing the preconditions of each action (e.g., I can only buy gas if I can afford the price) and deterministic consequences (if I buy ten thousand litres of gas then the station’s storage tank will increase by that much, until it hits its maximum capacity). As the real world typically contains deterministic ongoing processes, we also learn fixed rules for these dynamics (e.g., a rule capturing the business’ automated mortgage payments).
Improving Predictive Accuracy, Speed, and Planning Ability

Evaluating CASSANDRA on version 4.1 of the challenging MAPs business decision making environment, we accomplish a 20x speed up in prediction compared to prior work while halving the prediction error of stochastic variables. This improved modelling and speed translates to significant improvements in planning. Converting our world models into agents using Monte-Carlo Tree search, we find that Cassandra reliably accomplishes a 100% survival rate over the 50-day horizon – unlike all other methods that had a survival rate below 50%, and as low as 8%.

Figure: CASSANDRA exceeds in the MAPs business decision making environment, consistently surviving for the full horizon of the game, unlike other world models or ablations without the causal graph which become insolvent in over 50% of runs.
The Future: Lightweight and Interpretable Models for Text & Tabular Planning in Business

Through clever choices in representations, the relevant commonsense knowledge and world priors of LLMs can be distilled into fast interpretable systems that combine the perfect reliability of symbolic rules with neural networks’ flexibility in fitting to data. CASSANDRA leads the way, trailblazing a new paradigm for creating enterprise world models suited to structured text or tabular data. By scaling CASSANDRA’s rule and structure learning systems and combining them with hierarchical approaches, this will enable us to unleash the full power of traditional planning methods through the knowledge and reasoning of LLMs, producing fast and interpretable systems that are performant, require minimal data to train, cheap to run, and enable safety and constraint checking. Our team is working on making this a reality.
